speechtext:
I rise for the purpose of opposing the adoption of this report. The report, which will be found on page 2138 of Hansard of April 8th last, reads as follows:
The select standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines beg leave to present the_ following as its eleventh report.
Your committee has considered the following resolution referred to it:
That, in the opinion of this House, the time has arrived for the commencement forthwith, and the completion in the near future of a direct railway outlet from the Peace River country to the Pacific coast.
Your committee, having heard evidence on the subject matter of the resolution from the premiers of Alberta and British Columbia and from engineers who have investigated this project, and others, is of opinion that building a western outlet from the Peace River area is feasible from an engineering standpoint.
_ The weight of evidence before your committee indicates that, on economic grounds, such construction should not be commenced forthwith, as set forth in the resolution referred to your committee.
Your committee is of opinion that much greater traffic development is necessary in the area to make the building of such outlet economically sound.
Your committee is further of opinion that potentialities of that area are such as to warrant a continuous study of its development.
All of which is respectfully submitted.
It is not my intention to take up very much of the time of the House in connection with this matter, especially in view of the fact that so many hon. members-nearly ail of them in fact-have been working so hard and for such long hours during the last ten

Peace River Railway
days in order to finish the business of the session. But I cannot allow the report as it has been presented to go unchallenged, because I cannot agree that' it correctly interprets the evidence that was adduced before the committee. I am in general agreement with regard to the paragraph which states that a western outlet from the Peace river area is feasible from an engineering standpoint, although certain evidence was brought out before the committee in this connection that ought to be called to the attention of the House, because it affects to some extent the additional clauses in the report. The engineers commenced their report with these two paragraphs :
The undersigned were instructed to outline tile engineering and economic features of the various proposed [DOT] railway routes for a western outlet of the Peace river country to the Pacific coast.
A map showing the location of the various routes, giving distances, gradients, and other physical features would be of very little use, unless information as to costs of construction and comparable costs of operation were also given. We therefore have embraced in this report an economic study of the various routes considered.
We have a definite comparison of three routes any of which might be built to serve the Peace river country with an outlet to the Pacific coast. After having listened to the evidence, I claim that the engineers never made an engineering study outlining the engineering features of the various routes proposed. The first route that was examined and reported upon in the report is the Obed route. The survey in connection with this route is complete and it was in charge of Mr. Hill of the Canadian National Railways. Mr. Hill's official title is exploration and locating engineer of the Canadian National Railways. With regard to this route we have the following evidence by Mr. Hill:
Q. Who did the work in these routes?-A. We had regular surveying parties run over them. On the Obed route we have a complete survey from one end to the other.
Q. A complete survey?-A. A complete triline survey.
Q. Not a reconnaissance?-A. Not a reconnaissance, but an instrumental survey.
Q. In that case, Mr. Hill, you are in a position to speak definitely when yt>u say that the new construction will be 204 miles from Aggie to Sturgeon lake and down to Obed?-A. Within a reasonable percentage.
Q. How much allowance is there for variation-either less or more?-A. We would not . want any more than-it would be within 10 percent, and probably within five per cent.
Q. And would you say the same thing for the capital investment?-A. Yes.
The point that I am making is, that, according to the evidence submitted by Mr. Hill who
was in charge of the Obed route survey, there is a complete survey of that route. One would think that in order to make a proper comparison of this route with any other it would be necessary to have the same kind of a survey, but we find that that is not the case. The next route referred to is the Monkman pass route. We have the following evidence given by Mr. Hill at page 16 of the report of the committee on railways and canals with regard to the Monkman pass route:
Q. Is this a final survey or a reconnaissance or a trial survey?-A. This is a reconnaissance.
Q. What is the difference between reconnaissance, trial and a complete survey; will you kindly explain that? What do you do in the case of a trial survey, for instance?-A. Well, a trial line is generally an instrumental survey; it is an accurate survey.
Q. A trial survey is accurate?-A. Yes.
Q. What is a reconnaissance survey?-A. Well, they just trust the man that goes over it.
Q. He goes out with a pack on his back, is that it?-A. Well, they have different forms of transportation.
Q. Is a reconnaissance survey a question, of making a trip there to see if it is at all likely a railway can be built?-A. Yes.
Q. A trial survey is a survey that actually gives you the level?-A. Actually gives you the levels and the relative positions.
Q. What is tins Monkman pass survey? Is it a trial survey?-A. A reconnaissance.
Q. When we come to the question of costs and grades how re liable are these figures in connection with the Monkman pass as given in this report?-A. Jusc an engineer's guess, that is all.
So they make a comparison between one route, the Obed route, where there is a complete survey, and another route, the Monk-man pass route, Where we have an engineer's guess. The third route that was dealt with was the Peace River pass route. The gentleman who was in charge of this survey, such as it was, was Mr. W. A. James, assistant chief engineer of the Canadian Pacific Railway, who gave this evidence before the committee on railways and canals:
Q. You are the C.P.R. engineer who signed the report?-A. Yes, sir.
Q. Were you over the route from Spirit river right west through to Hudson Hope and from Berwyn west of Hudson Hope on the north side of the pass, and then through to Stewart?-A. On the north side of the pass I left Port George and went up to Summit lake and down the Crooked river, the Pack river and the Parsnip, down the Peace river to Peace River Crossing and then northwest from Peace River Crossing, which is a station on the Peace river, and then back to Peace river and to Carcajou point. I drove west from there and down paralleling the Peace river about 20 miles as far as Fort Vermilion, then I came up the Peace river from Fort Vermilion to Peace River Crossing again. I was over two months on that trip.
221.4
Peace River Railway

Q. You were actually over the route, were you?-A. Yes, sir.
Q. And the actual location of the railroad that is called Stewart to Prince Rupert and Vancouver via Peace pass?-A. I went by the Peace pass but I did not follow what you would call the actual route; I was on the river.
Q. We have no trial survey of this route, have we?-A. No, sir.
Mr. James made most of his exploration of this route from the Peace river which is in a valley 800 feet below the level of the territory to be served by the railway. As a matter of fact in the evidence he admits that as regards about 200 miles of the line that is projected on the map west to Stewart on the Portland canal, he was not over that route at all. We have what purports to be a serious comparison of the economic and engineering features of three routes, as regards one of which there is a complete survey and as regards the other two, we have simply engineers' guesses. The engineers claim to have made an engineering study and an economic study of these routes, but how can one claim to have made an economic study on the basis of an engineering study of that kind? This is the first time that I have ever known that a guess could be called a study. The two things are entirely different, and for that reason I am in complete disagreement with that paragraph of the report which reads:
The weight of evidence before your committee indicates that, on economic grounds, such construction should not be commenced forthwith, as set forth in the resolution referred to your committee.
As a matter of fact the resolution did not set forth that construction should be commenced forthwith. The wording of the motion is "commencement forthwith." Commencement does not necessarily mean actual construction of railway mileage, although I think as I go along I can show that even that will be justified.
In connection with this whole question there has been constant confusion as between the relation of the outlet and the branch line mileage. The Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning), in his speech on this question in the House of Commons, made this statement as reported on page 256 of Hansard of February 14, 1927, and I am in entire agreement with this part of his speech in which he refers to the need of 'branch lines:
[DOT]-but I think my bon. friend will also agree with we when I say that the problem is not in the main one of branch line construction to serve settlers now farming there. Only a relatively limited number of the farmers are now long distance from existing lines of transportation, and the problem is really one of providing a more economical way to the markets 
of the world for those situated within reasonable distance of those existing lines of transportation. I want to qualify that by saying that, as the engineers' report demonstrates, there is undoubtedly need for some further branch line construction on the Edmonton, Dunvegan and British Columbia system in order to enable the country to fully develop, in order to assist in its settlement and encourage immigrants, but in the main the problem is one of providing a more economical outlet to the people already there and within a reasonable distance of the existing lines of railway.
The outlet and the branch lines are not two separate and distinct matters at all; they are simply two parts of the same problem Everybody will agree that that part of the outlet that would best serve the Peace river country in the way of branch line mileage would be the proper portion to build first, and I may say that it is because of the indefinite nature of the engineer's report that I would have to waive my pressure for the immediate commencement of construction of an outlet at the present time, because I do not believe that even an engineering st-udy of the outlet question has 'been made, to say nothing of the economic study, which must be based upon a proper engineering study.
We all know that that country is being served at the present time by the Edmonton, Dunvegan and British Columbia railway. We all know that the branch line mileage that will properly serve the country as it is settled to-day and connect with the Edmonton, Dunvegan and British Columbia railway, will not fit in properly with an outlet to the Pacific coast. Mr. Czowski admitted that in his evidence, and I think everybody will agree that a branch line system constructed with oqe outlet will not necessarily, and will not likely, fit in with another outlet. I do not wish to take time quoting from the documents in support of that, because I think it is generally agreed. What I ask at the present time is that a real study be made of the Monkman, the Peace, and the Pine passes, and that a definite policy be laid down with regard to the permanent development of the Peace river country and an outlet to the Pacific coast. Then we can lay down the branch line mileage that is necessary to serye the Peace river country as it exists today, or will exist in the near future, in such a way that our branch line mileage will fit in properly and economically with that Pacific coast outlet when it is built, but I submit that it is absolutely impossible for the government of the province of Alberta or of British Columbia or the Dominion government intelligently to lay down a system of branch lines that will be of the proper ceonomic

Peace River Railway
advantages to the Peace river country and the Dominion unless that policy is laid down with a full knowledge of where the Peace river outlet is going to be.
We all know the problem that has arisen in this Dominion because of the duplication of railways. We have an example of that west of Edmonton, where about 200 miles of track was torn up because duplication rendered one track absolutely useless. We want to avoid that thing in connection with the development of the Peace river country, and as a matter of fact the engineer's report shows that it can be avoided, because the estimate which they have worked out in connection with the various routes is based on the branch line mileage serving a country with about 6,000 acres of economic land in the Peace river country tributary to each line of railway, as compared with some 5,200 acres in the rest of the prairie provinces. I am anxious that we should study the question in the light of our past experience, in the light not only of our past mistakes but of our past successes, so that we may evolve a railway policy for the development of that country that will be best not only for its immediate future but for its ultimate future as well.
With regard to the contention that it is economically unsound to build an outlet at the present time, I have this to say: The engineer's report seems to lay down the principle, by inference at least, that until such time as the necessary tonnage is available to justify the route from its commencement, it is economically unsound to build. I know of no railway in the Dominion of Canada that has been built on that basis. I think it was stated years ago when the building of the Canadian Pacific railway was under discussion, that it would not pay for the axle grease used in running the trains across the prairies. Neither is the feasibility of the Hudson Bay railway being tested by that principle. I am quite sure that it was not the principle on which the feasibility of the Grand Trunk Pacific or the Canadian Northern was decided, nor is it the principle underlying the branch line program of the Canadian National Railways that was presented to parliament this year, because the roads are there referred to as development and colonization lines.
What I want, Mr. Speaker, and what I think is in the best interests of the country, is to complete the survey of these routes and have a policy determined upon so that we shall know where to build our branch lines, and let me say that once we have built a mile of branch line that fits in with a policy for a permanent outlet we can be said to have 32649-140

commenced construction of the Peace river outlet. In that sense I say that the time is ripe for the commencement of that outlet, for we need at least 100 miles of branch lines in that country.
It is the last clause in the committee's report to which I particularly object, reading:
Your committee is further of opinion that potentialities of that area are such as to warrant a continuous study of its development.
The previous clause reads:
Your committee is of opinion that much greater traffic development is necessary in the area to make the building of such outlet economically sound.
Now if the last clause of the committee's report is adopted by the House of Commons and the government, it will simply mean that we do not mean to do anything, because it obligates the House of Commons and the government to do more than every member of parliament is already obligated to do with regard to every problem facing the Dominion of Canada. A continuous study of the development of the Peace river country is an obligation upon all the members of this House without any report being submitted to us from the committee on railways and canals, just as a continuous study of the problems and development of the maritime provinces or of Ontario or Quebec is the duty of all members of this House, whether from the west or elsewhere. That is all that clause obligates the House and the government to do, and I submit that either a mistake was made in drafting this report, or else the report is an attempt to shelve this Peace river question.
With regard to tonnage, it was pointed out in the committee, I think, that the engineer's estimate was that in the years 1919 to 1923 we had moving out of the Peace river country about 48,000 tons of grain on the average each year. Then they set down the immediate traffic that would go to the Pacific at 35,000 tons.
The evidence of Premier Brownlee based on grain shipments up to I think March 31st of this year, shows that about 130,000 tons has gone out of the Peace river country in the last crop year, from an area of only 270,000 acres of land, and we have about 2,000,000 acres of land of the very same type in the Peace river country in the area served by railways or that can be easily served by branch railways. Again 50,000 tons of grain produced oni the Edmonton, Dunvegan and British Columbia railway in the years 1919 to 1923 about 150,000 revenue tons of other traffic and yet the engineers state in their

speechtext: Peace River Railway

economic study that only grain traffic is going to be considered in connection with this Peace river outlet. They seem to rule out altogether the development that would take place in the Peace river country as a result of the construction of additional branch line mileage and the ultimate completion of the outlet itself. I submit that the committee has not given proper consideration to the engineering and economic features, and that the House is not justified in adopting its report. This question is of great importance to Peace river. The report says that all we are going to do in the immediate future is to study and watch the development of the country. I am glad the Prime Minister is in his seat, because he was not present when I spoke on this question before. I do not think we can say that the Prime Minister's statement cannot mean anything in view of the findings of the engineers, or the recommendations of the president of the Canadian National Railways. I am going to read again the statement made by the Prime Minister at Edmonton, and I hope that if he votes against the amendment which I propose to move, and for the report of the committee, he will at least tell the House, and especially the people of Peace River and Edmonton, what this statement meant. This statement appears in the Edmonton Bulletin of 11th October, 1924-I think it should be 12th October-and is headed:
King pledges self to Peace river cause.
Then there is a heading:
Premier promises outlet to Pacific.
Then sub-headings as follows:
Just as soon as humanly possible.
Railway will be built, declares Prime Minister at mass meeting here.
Government has but minority in Commons, says times now are different and everybody must have a little patience, but Liberal party is not falling down on any of its pledges.
The quotation reads:
"It is the policy of the government of which I have the honour to be the head to introduce a vigorous policy of immigration which will people the vast areas of undeveloped country in the great west" declared the Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King, Premier of. Canada, when addressing a mass meeting of citizens in the First Presbyterian church last night.
The future prosperity of this country is bound up in the development of its great natural resources, and to develop these resources it is necessary to have a large increase in the population of Canada. There is to the north of this city a great tract of land that is crying out for development. The Peace river country is amongst the richest in Canada, but before the proper development of that country can take place an outlet to the Pacific coast is an absolute necessity. I pledge myself that as soon

as it is humanly possible the great Peace river country will be given that measure of railway relief that will bring to the pioneers of that country the outlet they have been so long denied, and will open up the country for prospective settlers.
"I must however, sound the same note to you here as I did to the citizens of Saskatoon."
I suppose that is in connection with the Hudson Bay railway.
"The times that we are passing through are very difficult, and I would ask you to have a little patience, and in as short a time as possible, a railway outlet will be provided for the Peace River and northern Alberta districts that will open up an era of prosperity for that country which will not be equalled by any other province in Canada."
In view of the Prime Minister's promise, in view of the needs for additional branch line settlement, some of the settlements being twenty, thirty and sixty miles from' the railway, where there has been settlement for sixty years, and in view of the fact that branch line mileage cannot be constructed economically and properly unless we know where the Peace river outlet is going to be, and because I believe that such branch lines should be laid down as a part of the outlet, I am opposed to the adoption of this report and I therefore move the following amendment:
That the said report be not now concurred in but that the same be referred back to the select standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines with instructions that they have power to amend it by striking out the three following paragraphs:
"The weight of evidence before your committee indicates that, on economic grounds, much construction should not be commenced forthwith, as set forth in the resolution referred to your committee.
Your committee is of opinion that much greater traffic development is necessary in the area to make the building of such outlet economically sound.
Your committee is further of opinion that potentialities of that area are such as to warrant a continuous study of its development."
And substituting the following three paragraphs therefor:
"The evidence shows that there are four possible outlets but that a complete survey has been made of two only.
"Your committee is of the opinion that a complete survey should be undertaken of the Peace pass. Pine pass, and Monkman pass and that on completion of this survey a definite policy of railway development for the Peace river country should be decided upon.
"Your committee further believes that the potentialities of the Peace river district justify the commencement of a permanent outlet as soon as the best route is definitely ascertained."

maintopic: LIVE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK PRODUCTS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: As a matter of fact there is far more chance of exploiting the people of Canada with ungraded bacon than of exploiting the people in the Old Land, because our bacon going over there comes directly into competition with Danish bacon as well as meat from other countries, and must conform to a fairly high standard. maintopic: LIVE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK PRODUCTS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: For the sake of argument I will agree with my hon. friend, but it is still more important to preserve intact the concurring legislation, of the different provinces, for the time being.

maintopic: LIVE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK PRODUCTS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: I am sorry the minister cannot see his way clear to allow this bill to go through as it came from the committee. The bill was approved by the committee exactly as it was brought in here, and these few words which prohibit the grading of meat products in Canada in reality take away the entire effect of the bill. We have passed acts for the grading of fruit, and for the grading of wheat, but when it comes to the live stock, to which the farmers feed their grain, there will be no grading at all if these two words "for export" are inserted in this bill. I think the time has arrived when the principle of grading live stock and live stock products should be established. Perhaps the time is not opportune for the enforcement of grading; perhaps that can only be brought about gradually. But a year will elapse before we shall have another opportunity of amending this bill if it goes into law, and I think, therefore, that we should now establish the principle of grading live stock both for export and for home consumption. I should be sony to see a backward step taken in that regard; but I am afraid that if something is not done we are going to jeopardize the beef industry and seriously injure the bacon trade as well. I would urge the minister to allow this bill to go through as it came from the committee. Afterwards he can, by regulation, bring the act into force as he sees fit. In my opinion that would be the best course for him to pursue.

maintopic: LIVE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK PRODUCTS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: I agree with most of what my hon. friend has said. I should like to see the bill worded that way too, but it must be remembered that we are cooperating in team play with the provinces on this question. One of the most important provinces of the Dominion has drawn attention to the fact that this bill goes further, and in a more radical direction, than it did before, and that there has been no conference on the subject either with that province, or any of the other two provinces that were represented at the recent conferences at Regina and Ottawa. We all know the difficulty that we had in the matter of the grading of eggs. The greatest difficulty has been overcome but perhaps it would not have been but for the teamplay in that case also. I feel satisfied that we should do everything we can to avoid the possibility of weakening the confidence of the provincial governments, all of which have passed concurrent legislation, or of breaking faith with them. If the proposed legislation went through and it affected the principle of grading for the retail trade any of the provinces could say: You have defaulted in your undertaking with us by taking this authority. That is the point I wish to have borne in mind. But for that I should be inclined to leave the wording as it is. But adherence to the assurance I have given is of far more importance to me than having the two words in question left in the bill. There must be teamplay with the provinces if we are going to do the best work possible.

ticularly those who are away from home a good part of their time and have to depend on the tender mercies of people who provide provender for politicians throughout this country-have all experienced the fact that there is a great deal of tough beef placed on the table in Canada. After experiencing this for a number of years I have come to the conclusion that we are a strong-jawed, hardy race in this L)ominion, Now while it is very desirable that we should have grading applied in this country at the earliest possible moment, both to meats that are being exported and also to meats for local consumption, let me say that we should first have a clean-cut plan. Before we attempt to put this legislation into effect, let us have something to offer. Those countries that have been carefully investigating the grading of meats, particularly the United States, have not yet got a definite plan that can be applied; and what they are doing at the present time is to carry on experimental work hoping that something may be evolved from their investigations that will be of practical value. I would urge for Canada that this amendment be passed so that before going farther we may have the benefit of the experience gained in the grading of meat for export. After grading these meats for export for a year, or a year and a half, or two years, we shall be in the possession of much more knowledge than we have at the present time, and with that as a basis, we can introduce such legislation as will have a practical effect in improving the quality of beef in this country. This is a most important matter because at the present moment the consumer is as a rule a very poor judge of the quality of meat. In the first place this legislation when brought into force will have the effect of offering to the man who is willing to pay a little higher price for quality, an opportunity to secure what he wants, &nd that price will be reflected back to the man who produces on the farm. Tne general trend of the whole legislation is first-class but we should not attempt to put such legislation through now without a clean-cut, definite plan which we can apply with reasonable assurance of success.

speechtext:
If we can grade meat for
export, why can we not apply the same grades to meat that is to be sold at home?

maintopic: LIVE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK PRODUCTS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
We export about 15 per
cent of our cattle and we consume about 85 per cent at* home. Is it not much easier to try out our new plans on the smaller quantity of export meat than to try it on what is consumed at home? After a year or a year and

hive Stock Act
a half of experiment in this regard we can amend all those parts of our legislation that' are not practical, and from our experience during that period we can evolve something that will be of real use in connection with handling the larger quantity.

maintopic: LIVE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK PRODUCTS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Following up the argument of my hon. friend (Mr. Tolmie), I would say that there is no mandate from this committee to the Minister of Agriculture to conduct an investigation should these words " for export " that are referred to be inserted after the word " meat " in paragraph (i) of section 2 of the proposed legislation. We would place those words there for no other reason than to stall off a thorough investigation, whereas if the bill is passed as it now reads, we should have ample opportunity to take one, two or even three years to investigate the matter thoroughly. This will be enforced by regulations and it is entirely in the hands of the department to issue those regulations when they see fit". In order that a thorough investigation may be conducted, I think this particular paragraph should remain as it is now printed.
The minister spoke of breaking faith with some of the provinces. I should like for a minute to review some of the work of the department. The department have very efficiently introduced in connection with nearly all live stock products a grading system whereby they are educating the producers to turn out a high quality product. After the quality product is put on the market, the producer has to accept the mean average price for his product although it is superior to the product of which the exminister (Mr. Tolmie) spoke. In keeping faith with the provinces, let us not lose sight of the fact' that we should also keep faith with those who have gone to considerable expense in producing this high class product. I have correspondence, telegrams, from producers in western Canada urging the very thing for which this legislation calls, and I would impress upon the minister the necessity of seriously considering their request. No drastic change will be brought about if he takes plenty of time to investigate the matter before he issues regulations in order to cany this out immediately. I would strongly urge upon him to consider seriously the fact that t'he live stock men of this country are vitally interested in this matter. They have gone to great expense; they have studied the situation, and they are becoming discouraged in producing a high-class product. I am not speaking only for one section of the country; I have been in touch with many sections, and this is the impression I have gained. I have correspondence speaking very favourably of this particular clause as it
now stands, and I would urge upon the minister, if he can see his way to do so, to let the clause go through as it is now printed.

speechtext:
I wish to get the

speechtext:
I think the main
feature, at least from my standpoint, has been lost sight of. The provinces have entrusted to the Dominion the making of certain regulations regarding farm products, the understanding being that before any radical changes are made, we shall consult with them as to what those changes will be. We consulted with them in regard to all the rest of this legislation, but we did not consult with them in regard to this particular phase. It did not catch my eye at the time this bill was being drafted or it would not have appeared without the words "for export." The future of this legislation depends upon our living up to our agreement with the provinces.
I cannot make the matter any plainer. Since the bill was introduced I have received a letter from the Hon. Mr. Martin drawing my attention to the fact that this change was not considered when I was consulting him in regard to the matter. We have everything to gain and nothing to lose by playing fair. Before two years pass by this bill is bound to be up again, because a number of new phases agreed to by all parties will be introduced into it. Before this legislation comes up again I shall have an opportunity of consulting not only Mr. Martin and Mr. Caron but every other provincial minister of agriculture, and then we shall have an opportunity of making changes in accordance with the wishes of everybody. Without their consent this legislation is a dead letter and we do not want to give them any excuse for withdrawing their consent.

speechtext:
Is the legislation not

speechtext: Without the concurrence of the provinces it is. There are two decisions against the act.

maintopic: LIVE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK PRODUCTS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
We share the opinion
of our friends across the way that it would be well to have our products graded, but the matter is placed before us in a very reasonable way by the Minister of Agriculture when he says that, legislation on this subject having been held to be ultra vires, it is of first importance that we should have an agree-

ment and come to a common understanding with the departments of the several provinces. Otherwise, as the minister has said, this legislation W'ill be of no avail.

maintopic: LIVE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK PRODUCTS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: If this section stays in the act as it is, and the proper regulations are drawn up, none of the provinces will be hurt, and it will not be breaking faith with the men at all.

speechtext: This request of the minister this morning looks like another case of special privilege to a certain class.

maintopic: LIVE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK PRODUCTS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Well, we provide for the grading of practically all other products, and I do not see why this should not come into line. Some years ago when this matter was discussed in the committee of agriculture, the then member for South Oxford made a splendid argument for the inspection of all meats. It is a fact, I believe, to-day that at times our packers import a certain class of hog from the United States. I think we call them razorbacks for short, though they are more adapted for speed than bacon, as a rule. This meat is handled in such a way that it will not stand inspection, and I say to this House that the people of Canada do not know what they are getting on their breakfast table. I would like to see the House pass this measure. If it is found to work any injustice upon the packers, they can come back to the House in a year or two and have it corrected.

maintopic: LIVE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK PRODUCTS ACT AMENDMENT

Yes. My original intention was to let the bill go through the House the way it went through the committee, but I have since had communications from the Hon. Mr. Martin. I would be pleased to put them on record, but I have not his permission. However, I have shown the correspondence to a number of hon. members on the other side of the House, and I must say that his request seems to me very reasonable. It will not make any difference as to the results, but it will have a tremendous effect on the team play between the provincial and federal governments. I think this is the first time in the history of Canada that the nine provinces have passed practically the same concurrent legislation as the federal parliament. It is an experiment, and are we going to spoil it all at the very first opportunity by breaking faith with the provinces? There is something far bigger in those two little words "for export" than the question of whether we shall grade for export only or for home consumption as well, and that is the question, shall we be able to carry on along these lines in the future if we -break faith now? hive Stock Act

speechtext: I would like to point out to the hon. member for Rosetown who has referred to this "speed" bacon, that in the exchange of meats between the United States and Canada we have a mutual arrangement whereby the meats coming in from the United States bear the brand of the Bureau of Animal Industry, and our meats going into United States bear our government brand, so there is no question at all as to the wholesomeness of these products.

maintopic: LIVE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK PRODUCTS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I would like to point out to
my hon. friends who are opposing this amendment that the issue is not simply shall we have the inspection of meats intended for export or of ail meats, but rather, shall we have an inspection of export meats or no inspection ait all? That is the inevitable result of refusing this amendment. I am not interested in the grading of beef, but I am interested in the grading of eggs, and there was a decision given by Mr. Justice Grant last October, I 'believe, in connection with egg grading in Ontario that the whole of this act was ultra vires as it concerned domestic and inter-provincial matters, and not only the grading regulations but everything provided under the act fell flat. That had an immediate effect in British Columbia. I had an interview with the minister, and it was found that wre could not bring into force the egg grading regulations of the Dominion unless the provinces passed concurrent legislation. The minister was able to get all the provinces to pass concurrent legislation', very much to my surprise. As he says, it is almost a new departure for all the provinces to pass concurrent legislation with the Dominion. If we pass the act without this amendment it will mean that one or more provinces will break loose and be no longer bound by this agreement, and then not simply this particular section goes, but the whole act goes by the 'board so far as domestic and inter-provincial trade is concerned. So it is not a question of whether we shall have beef grading in the provinces, but whether we shall or shall not have export grading, because this act does govern exports, but it will not produce the results hon. gentlemen want unless we have this amendment. Without it, the whole thing will be in peril. I have no doubt that the minister will submit this matter to the Ontario Agricultural department during the next few months, and probably he will get their consent.

speechtext: I think the hon. member for Comox-Albemi is rather mixing up eggs and beef.

think there are good grounds for striking out beef altogether, because if the minister is going to grade beef for export and not beef for home consumption, you will find that the best beef will be exported and the tough beef will be left at home for Canadians to eat. No packer would ask to have his product graded for export if he thought it would be graded No. 3, and he will take care that what he ships for export will be of No. 1 grade. But I am not going to oppose the minister's amendment any further, because I see that he has certain grounds for asking for it. I think, however, he could facilitate the acceptance of the amendment if he would pledge himself within the present year to ask the different provincial departments of agriculture to agree to such legislation being passed.

speechtext: Surely. I will do my best.

maintopic: LIVE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK PRODUCTS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: If he will agree to that and give us their answers next year, so far as I am concerned I am perfectly willing to allow the amendment to pass. I think, however, the House is agreed that if it is desirable to have meat graded for export, meat for home consumption should also be graded.

maintopic: LIVE STOCK AND LIVE STOCK PRODUCTS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I understand
from what the minister says that there was a conference held in western Canada between the representatives of the producers' associations and the departments of agriculture in the western provinces. I know that a similar conference was held in eastern Canada, and that the representatives of the producers in eastern Canada are in favour of this bill being passed as it is now before the House. I have no doubt this bill was drafted after these two conferences had taken place at which everything was threshed out, and it seems to me rather strange that we should first of all have the bill provide for the grading of all meat products, which was approved by the committee, and then suggest this amendment when the only persons to object probably were the representatives of the packers and the live stock exchanges. I aim thoroughly convinced that the representatives of the producers want this bill to pass in its present form. It may be a few packers or representatives of the slock exchange do not think it is in their best interests to have it pass. I think a good deal of the opposition is coming from that quarter-from interests Which are against the producers of live stock in this country. We have to consider both. I think that the principle should be established in this bill that all meat should be graded and regulations brought in as conditions warranted in the years
hive Stock Act

to come. It has been pointed out that the provinces must pass concurring legislation before this bill will become effective. We must have something to work to in the future if we are going to improve our live stock, and unless we establish the principle of grading and showing the producer where he can obtain more for a first-class beast when he produces it we are not going to improve the live stock industry of the country as we should. It is a question of dollars and cents. If a man can feel that it pays to produce good stock he will produce it. We may talk about grading and publish pamphlets and do all we like to try and convince the producer that it is a good thing to produce a first-class article, but unless he can receive some compensation for his efforts when he sells his animal, the argument is largely in vain. We have to tackle this question at, some time; we should establish the principle now and work out the regulations in the years to come as they can be worked out in conjunction with the various provinces.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: SUPPLY-OIL AND GAS RIGHTS IN WESTERN CANADA
speechtext:
The
item we are considering is:	Cadet services,
$500,000. When the committee rose at six o'clock on Saturday evening an amendment had been moved by Miss Macphail to reduce this item by $499,999.

maintopic: SUPPLY-OIL AND GAS RIGHTS IN WESTERN CANADA
speechtext:
In rising to speak to the question, in order to avoid making a number of short speeches, I propose to discuss briefly not only this item but the estimates for national defence in general. Before doing so I wish to join with the hon. member for Winnipeg North Cdntre (Mr. Woodsworth) in congratulating the House upon having obtained the services of the hon. gentleman who administers the Department of National Defence (Mr. Ralston). I am sure that the minister's genial and affable manners, and the clear and lucid way in which he speaks have earned for him the admiration and respect of hon. members in all corners of the chamber. And then, in connection with our opponents, may I say that after all it appears to me we are both working for the same end. They think that peace will be attained and maintained by the methods which they
32649-Hli
propose, while we here, who are just as sincere in our desire for peace, think it will be best secured by other means than those which they advocate.
Now in regard to the cadet movement, I think, perhaps that the most objectionable feature is the fact that it is supervised by a military officer in the schools; and after all the objections that have been stated by the hon. member for Southeast Grey (Miss Macphail), and the leader of the Labour party in this House (Mr. Woodsworth), I think it is only fair that we should look at the question from all angles. The responsibility for the cadet movement does not rest with the Dominion government, nor does all the opposition to the cadet movement come from a few cranks, shall I say, in the House of Commons. There is no doubt that there is a concerted movement among the churches, and among other bodies, protesting very loudly, very sincerely and very emphatically against the cadet movement in this country.

maintopic: SUPPLY-OIL AND GAS RIGHTS IN WESTERN CANADA
speechtext: Cite a number of those that are protesting.

maintopic: SUPPLY-OIL AND GAS RIGHTS IN WESTERN CANADA
speechtext:
I could cite several, for
instance the United Church of Canada in the province of Alberta has gone on record as protesting against such things. I need not name all the particular organizations which have done the same. I simply mention the fact to show that the movement is not confined to a few labour cranks in this corner of the House.

maintopic: SUPPLY-OIL AND GAS RIGHTS IN WESTERN CANADA
speechtext:
The hon. member spoke
of "churches". What other church has protested?

maintopic: SUPPLY-OIL AND GAS RIGHTS IN WESTERN CANADA
speechtext:
I said I did not wish to give a list of all the people that are protesting. I will simply add that I have received a number of letters along that line and leave the question there. At the same time it is only fair to say that the whole responsibility for this movement does not rest upon the Dominion government. It is optional-and it is only fair to put it that way-with the provincial governments to take what stand they please in the matter; and I am rather sorry to say-I wish to be absolutely fair-that I believe the Farmers government of Alberta have failed to make a protest against the cadet movement in connection with the schools of that province. The cadet movement is not a compulsory matter. If any school desires to adopt the cadet movement it is open to it to do so, if a school does not wish to take it up its wish will be respected. Therefore wherever the cadet movement ob-
2232	COMMONS
Supply-Defence-Cadet Services
tains, responsibility must be shared by the province, the schools and the homes; it should not be fastened solely upon the members of the Dominion government or the members of this House. There appears to be a feeling that the opposition to the cadet movement is inspired by antagonism to the returned men. I want to say that there is no such attitude in my own mind. There is an old saying that "It is an ill bird that would foul its own nest"; and in view of my own experience in 1914, when I and a number of others marched down the streets seeing our own sons off to the war, it would ill become me to cast any reflection whatsoever upon the men who have returned from the war. As for the returned men, I believe the last thing they want in their inner hearts is another war such as the one that was brought to a conclusion in 1918.
In the discussion the other day an hon. gentleman to my right presented a simile to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. He said to him "Would you not insure your house against fire"? and of course the answer came "yes". "Well," the hon. member in question said, "the military and naval organizations are an insurance against a conflagration of the kind of which you are speaking." I take issue with that position right now, and I wish to carry out the simile to what I believe to be its logical conclusion. Let us take it for granted that we are trying to insure ourselves, as well as our sons and our grandsons, against such a conflagration as occurred in 1914. Now when a fire occurs we do not damn the firemen but we curse the fire. We do not seek to cast any reflection against the fire brigade, but we try to remove all combustible materials lying around that would permit that fire to spread. So in this case we do not damn or condemn the soldiers, but we do most heartily damn and condemn war. Our object should be to use preventive measures in order to prevent the occurrence of these things in the future.
One of the first things a fire insurance company does is to come around the house and see if there is anything that might cause a fire and, if so, it asks that it be removed. If in a city there was a large fire and if some time after the fire you saw combustible materials lying around from which there was danger of another fire, you would not simply go to the city council and say: Let us increase the fire brigade; let us increase the number of fire engines. They would say: That is foolish; let us remove those combustible materials. That will be the proper procedure in that regard.

Let me carry this question a little further. If you had a fire so serious that it had devoured half your buildings and half your fire brigade, and if experts came to you some years afterwards and pointed out that the aggregation of combustible material was becoming so dangerous that, if another fire broke out, not only would all the buildings bo destroyed, but the whole fire brigade and the whole city would go up in smoke, what would be your answer? What would be your earnest endeavour, the earnest endeavour of any serious-minded, sensible man? Would you go once more to the city council and say: Gentlemen, let us increase the fire brigade; let us increase the number of fire engines? No, the fire insurance companies would insist that you bend your efforts to removing the combustible material that might cause another fire. Their answer would be this: The next fire will be so far beyond you that no fire brigade, no fire engines, will ever be able to extinguish it and the city and the city brigade will all go up in smoke. Therefore, applying that as a principle, we should bend our utmost efforts to remove from Canada and an fact the world at large those combustible things that might cause such another war conflagration in which not only the fire brigades, that is the armies, but our citizens and civilization itself would be swallowed up.
I wrant to read just a few extracts so as to turn the attention of the committee to what I consider is the most serious thingt in regard to war. I am not speaking of my own authority; I have in my hand a message from no less a gentleman than Sir Oliver Lodge, who, in speaking about these combustible materials in Europe and indeed the world at large, made this. statement. He appealed to "world statesmen to curb the international tendency to produce instruments of destruction." A chair of pacifism has been established at Kiel university. Doctor Walter Sehuecking, member of the Reichstag, has been assigned to Kiel by the Prussian Ministry of Education as professor of international law and of the history of international pacifism.

So far as Canada is concerned, so far as I am concerned, not for myself but for my children and grandchildren, for the children
of my neighbours and their children's children, what are we doing in the direction of peace? The estimates show that we are appropriating about $13,000,000 for this year for military armaments iand services, for the fire brigade, if you like. I will leave that question in abeyance. What are we doing for the prevention of another war conflagration? I have looked all through the estimates and on page 61 I find the only mention of peace:
Grant to the Inter-parliamentary Union for Peace, $200.
There is the magnificent sum of $200 for peace. My protest to-day is perhaps not so much against the items that we have in the estimate of the Department of National Defence although part of my protest is against that. I say that we ought to wake up to the danger and not live in a fool's paradise; that we should do what any sensible fire insurance company would do, what any sensible man would do if the whole city was surrounded by combustible material. We should bend our best efforts to endeavouring to prevent such a conflagration rather than to cure it after it has taken place. It is said that an ounce of prevention is better than a pound of cure." The whole tendency in medical science is to prevent sickness rather than to cure it. In forest conservation the idea is to prevent fires rather than to put them out after they have started. So I would plead with the House to make for the maintenance of peace at least half the appropriation that we are making for protection against war.

The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre in those trying days, when that peaceable strike took place, took very few risks himself. Seeing that he was a Canadian-born citizen he ran no risk of being deported. In regard to going into prison, I quote his statement at Calgary under date of October 29, 1919:

There is not a great deal of courage behind a statement like thatl He wants to gain control of the military and the courts in this country, so we can understand why he is opposed to the item at present before the committee. I do not intend to detain the committee any longer than to say this:	I
quoted from Kipling a little while ago and I have given indications of what Kipling perhaps had in mind when he said:
And the things that you learn
From the yaller and brown
'll 'elp you a lot with the white.
The things we have learned not from "the yaller and the brown," but from white gentlemen who have given their encouragement, at least not their discouragement, to such things as took place in Winnipeg in 1919, will help us a lot in managing the affairs of this country, if we only properly appreciate what they did or attempted to do and keep them in their place.
It has been my misfortune during this debate to refer to another hon. member, the hon. member for Southeast Grey (Miss Mac-phail) in a way which evidently that hon. member did not approve. I have nothing whatever to say against the person who represents Southeast Grey. When I refer to that hon. member I am referring to the person who represents the constituency of Southeast Grey, just as I would refer to any other member in this House who represents any other constituency. I am speaking, not against the personality of the one who made the remarks any more than against the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, but against the teachings and the general attitude of mind of the hon. member for Southeast Grey, which I think are not in the best interests of the Dominion of Canada. I would not have said so much about the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre if he had confined his remarks to Winnipeg North Centre. But he has been speaking in various parts of this country and I want the people of Canada to understand him as I think I do. I would refer him to a statement which he made as reported on page 1732 of Hansard of last year in reference to singing the national anthem. He said
I remember that I became conscious that the tune was "God Save the King", but I paid no attention.
I represent people of the opposite class. When I recognize the fact that the national anthem is being sung I feel like standing to attention as I believe all loyal subjects will do, and in that way showing my respect for the head of the British empire.
It was my misfortune to bring down upon my head the wrath of the hon. member for Southeast Grey. In that connection I will close by saying that if before I came here this afternoon I did not appreciate the truth of Kipling's statement, I certainly do now when he said:	"The female of the species
is more deadly than the male."

speechtext:
Having
listened to the provocative speech of the hon. member (Mr. Edwards, Frontenac), there will be no longer any wonder in the minds of those who have wondered in the past why Ireland was such a distressful isle. The hon. gentleman has undoubtedly ability to stir things up and I think he has succeeded this afternoon. The reverberations of his utterances will not for some time cease to sound throughout this chamber. However, not having been referred to personally by that person I am not going to take issue with him because on this particular item of the estimates, while I may be no more obtuse than others, I did not hear him produce any worthwhile arguments as to why we should keep on increasing our appropriations for cadet training or for other military purposes.
I would like to ask hon. gentlemen and the minister concerned: What after all do we gain by the enormous increase in our military esti-
2242	COMMONS
Supply-Defence-Cadet Services
mates this year? I have in my hand an editorial from a humble western newspaper, one of those little things that crop up from time to time showing signs of reasoned intelligence and logic. This paper which is called the Western Producers has this to say on the question of the advantages or disadvantages of continuing to arm. It asks itself: What have we gained by arming? And on the basis of that question it writes this:
It is certain that there is a large and growing sentiment in Canada that the policy of individual nation-arming, with the hope of being able to conquer any possible foe at any time, is a hopeless task, and in contradiction to the spirit of the age. The policy adopted by the Navy League is the old policy governing the conduct of all nations at all times since the beginning of history. It is the policy which has failed to protect past empires and past nations. It is the policy that has brought on war and increased the ferocity of war. It is the policy that has led to intense national pride and consequent international bitterness. It is the policy that has destroyed millions of lives and devastated continents. It is the policy which the Great war was supposed to terminate. It is generally accepted that the policy has worked well for the British Empire-
Hon, gentleman to my right have argued that again and again:
-but even that may be subject to challenge. Great Britain, largely as a result of her naval and military preparations, has been swamped in taxes. It can be imagined that if Great Britain had devoted her brains and her money to social improvement and industrial development-
And I might add international harmony and brotherhood:
-the million or so men now out of work and miserable would he employed and happy.
One million is too small a figure. Other eminent economists have put the figure as high as ten millions out of work and unhappy :
England has protected her shores and her commerce, but she cannot protect millions of her citizens from starvation and abject squalor. Her freedom, as it is called, has been maintained, but the freedom enjoyed by the destitute families of desperate men, is a doubtful asset from the standpoint of the workless.
I ask again, whait do we hope to gain from this additional expenditure on armaments in this country? What excuse there was for Britain does not exist in this country. What excuse Great Britain might have had for adding to her army and navy and increasing her military and naval expenditures year after year does not exist in this country. We are in a geographical position that relieves us from the menace of European conflict. We have no enemies who wish to injure us. We have even the voice of some of the greatest statesmen that England has ever produced in

support of our attitude. No one questions the brilliance and depth of thought of Arthur Ponsonby, who during the MacDonald administration was Under-Secretary of Foreign Affairs. Referring to the dominions, in his book, Now is the Time, he has this to say, and I commend these words to the minister and to the administration at page 82:
Any disposition on the part of our dominions to refuse to join in these wars of European origin will be all to the good. The deadweight of a reasonable pacifism from that quarter might have a moderating effect on the home government.
There is no question about it:
If the jingo does not want the break-up of the empire, he must moderate his tone and abstain from converting inter-governmental disputes into causes of war. In any ease, however, so widely different are the circumstances-
This is the point I want to emphasize:
In any ease, however, so widely different are the circumstances of life and world relations in our dominions, that it can only be a matter of time for them to have complete control over their own destinies. For us to prevent them from reaping the inestimable benefits of peace which their great distance from the European powder magazine would naturally allow them, must indeed, sooner or later, strike both the governments and the peoples of the dominions as intolerable.
There are many other references pf like character in that volume and in other volumes that you can find; they were referred to by the hon. member for Southeast Grey when she was speaking. Lord Grey, Lord Milner, and many other of the greatest thinkers and statesmen that England has produced denounce the madness and insanity of war and of continuing preparations for war, because the result is always and inevitably the same. Some gentlemen sing of glory and victory and triumph. The hon. member for Frontenac this afternoon quoted Kipling. Let me answer him by quoting from one of our Canadian poets, Robert Service, in a volume dedicated to his brother, Lieutenant Albert Service, who was killed in action in France in August, 1916:
Victory! there can be but one, hallowed in every land;
When by the graves of our common dead we who were foemen stand;	.
And in the hush of our common grief hand is tendered to hand.
Triumph! Yes, when out of the dust in the splendour of their release
The spirits of those who fell go forth and they hallow our hearts to peace,
And, brothers in pain, with world-wide voice, we clamour that War shall cease.
Another tribute:
Glory! Ay, when from blackest loss shall be born most radiant gain;

Supply-Defence-Cadet Services
When over the gory fields shall rise a star that never shall wane;
Then and then only our dead shall know that they have not fall'n in vain.
When our children's children shall talk of war as a madness that may not be;
When we thank our God for our grief to-day, and blazon from sea to sea
In the name of the dead the banner of Peace .	.	.	. that will be Victory.
Yes, Mr. Chairman, and that is the direction in which I hope every effort of mine will be placed. In a peaceful country like this, without enemies, I do not want to see these estimates increased, for that increase in turn creates a psychology so inevitably drawing the nation sooner or later into military competition and into war itself. Would it not be much better that we should devote the moneys we have to other and worthier purposes? We find, for instance, that it is difficult for the returned men who fought in the last war to get the justice they feel is theirs. The Minister of Finance rose in the House on Saturday morning and referred in a very autocratic manner to the position which he was prepared to take if certain amendments to the Pension Act were not at once accepted. There are other questions that arise. There is need in this country for expenditure on post offices and other public works. There is need for expenditure in many districts that are awaiting development, to add to the prosperity and wealth of this nation, but we have no money for these things, while for war and preparations for war we have millions of dollars to spend.
I was interested enough to place on the order paper some little time ago an order for a return showing the total of appropriations for the fiscal year 1925-1926, both on capital and consolidated accounts. I asked that the figures be tabulated in various divisions showing, first, appropriations relating to past wars; secondly, appropriations relating to future wars, and other divisions showing expenditures on public works, science, social and ethical improvements, and so on. I received that return a little time ago. I have taken some trouble to analyse a part of it; I have not had time to go through the whole of it yet. But I find this: Cut of the 1925-1926 appropriation we spent for past wars, and this will practically be the same as this year, $163,639,165.24. We are now preparing for another war in that we are spending nearly $14,000,000; $13,774,805 to be exact, on military preparations. In order to get a fair idea of how our development is tending, let us see how much is being spent by the federal government on science. The total amount spent in all departments of government on science during that year was
the paltry sum of $2,944,000. How much was spent on social and ethical development? A total of $2,541,000. We spent $14,000,000 preparing for war, and $163,000,000 on account of past wars, and before we have measurably reduced our war debt, before we can spend hardly anything on science or on social and ethical development we are proceeding to add another $3,000,000 in one year to the military expenditures of this country. I do not think there is any defence that can be put up to support the hon. minister in the increase he is asking in these estimates this year, and I hope that when he speaks he will give us really worth while reasons that will appeal to common sense why this increase is being asked for.
I will give him another reason why there should not be an increase in these estimates. I have in my hand the Canadian Forum, one of our brilliant little publications in Toronto, whence other thoughts come than those emanating from the hon. member for Fron-tenac. One of the editors of this publication indicates that there is a psychological effect which is at once developed the moment we become a busily arming nation. He puts it this way:
But the cardinal argument against Canada, at this of all times, beginning to build up defensive forces is psychological. The success of the league is bound up with the cause of disarmament. It is true that as yet little has been done towards the limitation of armaments, and it is possible that the next disarmament conference will be little more successful than other attempts in the past.
But the forces working towards disarmament are strong and confident; we believe that they will triumph, because they represent the spirit of the age; but even those who have not that faith must admit that there are good grounds for hope that they prevail, although their first victory may not be until the time when France is faced with the near prospect of a Germany free to arm against her-and that time is not quite yet. At the present time and under these circumstances if Canada were to take measures towards arming herself, which she never previously considered, the adverse moral effect on world opinion might but out of all proportion to the importance of the measures taken.
I think that is only too true a statement. The adverse pyschological effect on the work of those who at the present time are pressing forward in the cause of peace is something the administration of this country might well pay some attention to.
Even if those measures were merely to make a direct contribution towards Britain's forces which would relieve her and leave the total British armament unchanged, the facts would be distorted by every enemy of the commonwealth and the league, perfidious Albion would again be painted in sinister colours on the front

Supply-Defence-Cadet Services
pages of every Anglophobe news-sheet, and the forces working for disarmament would suffer a definite reverse.
The administration might consider the value of that argument. To me it is a very powerful one. One of the greatest contributions this country can make to the cause of peace at the distance we are placed from the continent of Europe, free from the constant touch of hate that influences the feelings of our statesmen on the other side of the water, free to view matters in a broader way and clearer light and weigh up incidents that occur from time to time, and free as we are to bless ourselves with a peaceful future, is to encourage disarmament by our own example and so add weight to the efforts of others in foreign countries in this great cause. It is to be condemned that a country like thi3, with such vast possibilities for peace advancement in its own home, should now, in this of all years, increase to such an enormous extent the armaments of this country. There are many deplorable things coming from Toronto, but some good things too.

maintopic: SUPPLY-OIL AND GAS RIGHTS IN WESTERN CANADA
speechtext:
Has the hon. member
considered the present naval armament of Canada, consisting of one or two mine sweepers? Do you base any argument along that line?

maintopic: SUPPLY-OIL AND GAS RIGHTS IN WESTERN CANADA
speechtext:
I do not
think we need worry in the least about our navy and our army in this country unless it be demonstrated that the purpose can be served in line with the argument used by the hon. member for Frontenac. I fail to see why we should carry a burdensome, top-heavy army or naval force.
I have in my hand a communication which I received this morning from Toronto,
headed-
Fellowship of Canadian Youth for Peace.
When I read dt I had a glowing feeling of satisfaction. I felt that there was creeping into the people a realization of their destiny, and the need of the development of a desire for peace in the country. After all human nature is not what it is said to be. The healthy boy does not want to go out and kill. -All he does is to arm himself with a wooden sword because he sees pictures of armed soldiers, he sees pictures of men on horseback gaily decked in glittering war array. It is not with a desire to kill that he marches round. It is not to train for future conflict. But if you are going to band your boys together in the way proposed, give them real guns and show them the easy way in which they can destroy life, pleading speciously that IMr. E. J. Garland.]
they should only use these guns when occasion arises, you are creating the probability of the very thing we desire to avoid. A letter I have received this morning is in the following
terms:
I have the honour of sending you a copy of a resolution, which I am sending to the Minister of Militia on behalf of the Fellowship of Canadian Youth for Peace (Toronto Branch).
We hope you will give this communication your earnest consideration.
Yours sincerely,
(Mrs) Amy Guyot,
Secretary.
And the letter to the minister reads as follows:
Dear Sir,
With an ever increasing number of people becoming alive to the fact that the greatest and most important task of our generation is the abolition of war; and as in the words of the League of Nations Union, "armaments are the chief obstacle to goodwill and peace among the nations," this fellowship views with alarm the increase in the Military estimates for this country of over $3,000,000.
We believe that the only effective "defense" is by the promotion of international understanding and goodwill and suggest that all such money should be used for this purpose.
On behalf of the Executive Committee of the Fellowship of Canadian Youth of Peace (Toronto Branch).
Yours sincerely,
(Mrs.) Amy Guyot,
Secretary.
I add that to my contribution to Hansard as an indication of the development of a splendid psychological condition in the minds of the youth, at least, of one part of our country.
I now come to another stage in this matter. I have no doubt hon. gentlemen who support these estimates will support them for many reasons, among others those argued by Premier Bruce of Australia at the Imperial conference, and renewed by him when he visited this country shortly afterwards. He was eloquent about it when he came to Canada to instruct us as to what we ought to do as our contribution. Not having had an opportunity of concluding my speech on the Imperial conference to date, I wish to congratulate the Prime Minister on the speech he made in Toronto in which he deliberately and very splendidly castigated the Prime Minister of Australia for the unquestioned impertinence that that gentleman displayed when he came here to tell us what we ought to do in the matter of empire defence.
