I wish to finish my remarks, the hon. gentleman can speak later. He then proceeded to offer a great many figures. For example, he quoted Great Britain showing that the total per capita expenditure on war-that is the army and navy-was 51s. Id., but Canada was contributing only 5s. 10d., as compared with 51s. Id. He rebuked us very much for that, especially when he came proudly to announce that Australia was contributing 27s. 2d. for 1925-26, England 12s. lid., and South Africa 2s. 6d. I am glad to see that one country was slightly below us, or we would have got a dreadful spanking from Premier Bruce when he was here. If hon. members would look at Premier Bruce's figures from the point of view which, in my opinion, they should be looked at, they would not find so much to complain about, nor could we. Does anyone realize what it should cost us to maintain an armed force in order to be secure? Of course it is a form of insurance, just as we insure our buildings against fire and just as we insure our lives against death. We are endeavouring to insure against some danger. Does it not follow then that the nation in the greatest danger, in constantly present danger, would naturally pay a very greatly increased premium over those which would be paid by the nation that was not in any way in danger, or with, the possibility of danger so slight that it could be regarded as being almost negligible? It appeals to me that if more security is the basis for our armament this contribution Great Britain makes for her security, situated as she is in the midst of national hates, is not at all too high. On the other hand I refuse to admit that the contribution we make to our security is too low. In support of that I should like to quote from an article that appeared in the Manchester Guardian Weekly of Friday, March 18, 1927. It is headed, The Burden of Armaments-The Premiums paid for National Security, and is written by Walter G. Layton, editor of the Economist. The article is well worth reading. Mr. Layton has this to say:
It is surely very unsatisfactory that the removal of the menace of a world conflagration should not have been followed by a much greater easement of the burden of armaments 32649-142
than this. There is no way in which the taxpayer can hope to get a more substantial measure of relief than by a drastic cut in the scale of armaments as a result of the international conferences shortly to be held.
In this connection it is worth while pointing out the extent to which different countries are carrying the burden of armaments. According to the most recent and authoritative estimate, the national income of Great Britain in 1924 and 1925	(1926 was, of course, abnormal)
amounted to about 4,200 millions. Our expenditure on war preparations (including certain items carried on other votes than those of the three fighting services) amounted to well over 120 millions. In other words, the premium paid for insuring national security was three per cent.	[DOT]
Three per cent of the income was devoted as a form of premium to guarantee security in so far as armaments would do it; that arming does ever guarantee security is again debatable.
This is a slight improvement on 1913, when the premium worked out at three and a half per cent, but is much worse than in the last three decades of the nineteenth century, when a premium of about two per cent was all that was considered necessary. (It should be remembered, in passing, that while this is a perfectly reasonable method of representing the burden of armaments on the population of Great Britain, it is not a true index of the military effort of the British Empire; for the figure would work out at a much lower rate for the empire as a whole, seeing that the dominions are taxed for war purposes at a very much lighter rate than the mother country-namely one-half per cent to three-quarters per cent).
Now we come to this point:
At the present moment France is paying a premium of some three and a half per cent, with a war budget of nearly 5i milliard francs, as compared with a national income which M. Berenger put at 130 milliard francs, but is probably nearer 160 milliard francs. Italy is paying a security premium of over four per cent with a war preparation budget of over four milliard lire and a national income of about 100 milliard lire. The figures for Germany are in striking contrast, and her war expenditure, at 560 million marks out of a national income estimated by the Berlin Chamber of Commerce at 35,000 million marks, is equal to a premium of li per cent.
Of course, we all know why that is. Germany is not allowed under treaties to arm, on the scale she would like to. Otherwise I have no doubt the premium in her case would be higher.
This national income figure is, however, probably on the low side, and the premium therefore is rather less than this figure. The low-est premium of all the great powers is that of the United States,-
And this is where the comparison comes in. -which works out at about one per cent, the national income being at least 6,000 million dollars and defence expenditure under 600 million dollars.



Supply*-Defence-Cadet Services
The premiums naturally vary-like all forms of insurance premium-with the degree of risk, real or supposed, to which the insurer is subject; but it is fairly evident that the heaviest burden is being shouldered by those least able to bear it, and for this reason there is a real inducement for the nations of Europe to make a substantial reduction.
Now you have this situation. You have Italy with a four per cent' war premium, England with a three and a half per cent war premium and France with a four to five per cent war premium. Why? Because they are all centered in a seething caldron of hate, they are in the heart of a continent where the unfortunate injustices of past wars and past treaties have inflamed race against race until there is no hope of peace while that hate continues. This is in direct contrast' with the conditions on this continent, where we are free from that form of hate and are living in amity with the United States and the world. We are an industrious, peaceable people, and desire to remain so. I think to-day the greatest power in the world is the United States of America, and it pays a war premium of one per cent. Why? Because relatively she is secure in her geographic position. Then let us consider what should be the policy of Canada. Why should we be asked to pay the higher premium when we possess a security certainly equal to that of the United States of America?
I am satisfied because of our geographical position. We have the friendliness of those who are on one side of us, and our relations with world countries are always friendly- unless we happen to have been involved in unfortunate affairs of the mother country. We are not a quarrelsome people, we wish to trade with other countries, not to fight with them, and so long as Canadian resourcefulness and progressive thought continue, there is in my opinion no excuse, certainly no reason, for increasing in one single year our defence estimates by some $3,000,000. Nor do I think we are justified in adding to the armaments of this country for almost any reason whatever. I find hon. gentlemen t'o my right, and indeed a few opposite-not so many as there used to be, although there are still too many-prone to argue that after all human nature being what it is we must' prepare for war. They tell us, You cannot stop people wanting to fight. I am not so sure. I will admit that if the member for Frontenac-Ad-dington is around anywhere it sort' of helps to liven things up a little bit and we may not be able to keep out of the scrap as long as we otherwise would. But I cannot admit that human nature is the secret of these war preparations. I have watched children, including
tMr. E. J. Garland.]
my own, long enough to realize that there is no instinct in them to quarrel, no desire to kill one another. They like to play with flowers and with their fellow boys and girls, they love t'he sunshine and generally have a good time. What changes them is enrolling them into this sort of cadet training where they drill in stiff military attitudes and t'he Prussian spirit is developed in them. Then the little child becomes imbued with the war slogans, military jargon, the dreadful spirit of war that poisons life for him, and that some day or other he spews up in gasping death on the battlefield. That is the pitiful thing of it all. No one has put what I feel about this in better words than Shelley in his immortal Queen Mab, where he has this to say:
*-yet fear not;
This is no unconnected misery,
Nor stands uncaused, and irretrievable. Man's evil nature, that apology Which kings who rule, and cowards who crouch set up
For their unnumbered crimes, sheds not the blood
Which desolates the discord-wasted land. From kings, capitalists, and statesmen, war arose,
Whose safety is man's deep unbettered woe, Whose grandeur his debasement. Let the axe Strike at the root, the poison-tree will fall; And where its venomed exhalations spread Ruin, and death, and woe, where millions lay Quenching the serpent's famine, and their bones
Bleaching unburied in the putrid blast,
A garden shall arise, in loveliness Surpassing fabled Eden.
He turns then to the children and says again:
Nature! No!
Kings politicians, and statesmen, blast the human flower
Even in its tender bud; their influence darts Like subtle poison through the bloodless veins Of desolate society. The child, [DOT]	/
Ere he can lisp his mother's sacred name, Swrel!s with the unnatural pride of crime, and lifts
His baby-sword even in a hero's mood.
This infant-arm becomes the bloodiest scour-age
Of devastated earth: whilst specious names, Learned in soft childhood's unsuspecting hour, Serve as the sophisms with which manhood dims
Bright Reason's ray, and sanctifies the sword Upraised to shed a brother's innocent blood.
I wish, Mr. Chairman, I could have put into such immortal words my feelings in this matter. I will, however, express my opinion by voting in support of the amendment moved by the hon. member for Southeast Grey.

speechtext:
I have listened for two
days to the enunciation of principles to which I believe every hon. member of this House can subscribe, in relation to the horrors of war and the desire for peace, and I am sure there are hon. members of this House within reach of my voice who are just as anxious for peace and just, as intimate with the horrors of war as are any of tho hon. gentlemen who have so far spoken, one of whom made a magnificent contribution to the war. I refer to the hon. member for East Calgary (Mr. Adshead), to whom I 'wish to give great credit.
I want to say to you, Mr. Chairman, that I could make the speech which my hon. friend has made against war and in favour of peace, if I had his eloquence and his quotations, in the hope that the world would realize that seme day we must adopt this principle; and the next moment I could ask this House to vote the small amount which is being asked by the defence department of this country, because I believe the two things go hand in hand, and because I do believe the hon. members of this House and the people of this country do not quite realize exactly what is the duty which has been imposed upon your humble servant in filling this portfolio. I am presiding over the Department of National Defence, not over a department which has to do with the propagation of the principle of the abolition of war, and1 I do resent the remarks made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre when he said we have professional militarists whose job is in this thing, men who are at it in season and out of season, trying in every way to use their influence to perpetuate war. I say to my hon. friend that I do not believe that to be the
case in the Dominion of Canada, and that 1 have yet to meet a professional militarist. I say to him, Mr. Chairman, and to other hon. gentlemen, in all sincerity, that I believe at least ninety-nine per cent of the men in the Department of National Defence and in the militia generally throughout Canada would be delighted if the time came when this country could do without its defence forces and disband them entirely. I want to say further that so far as I am concerned this portfolio o: national defence is in the hands of my leader and of His Excellency the Governor General, because I do not propose to be here any longer than is absolutely necessary, in my humble judgment, to see that we have at least some form of defence such as that which is regarded as necessary having regard to conditions in the world.
Now let us get our heads out of the clouds, because I think we all admit and agree to the principles which my hon. friend has enunciated. Personally I was guilty on one occasion of using a good many quotations and a good deal of eloquence-and I was just as earnest and sincere as my hon. friend from Bow River-in delivering an address on international goodwill, and I say that I can occupy this portfolio and ask this House to vote these estimates while I still believe in every principle which I enunciated at that time. International goodwill is not being disturbed at all because some nations see fit to put a lock upon their front doors in the shape of a defence force within those particular countries. International goodwill is going to be maintained and furthered when we see to it that the will of war is uprooted from the hearts and minds of our people, and when we see to it that the things we have to say now, which perhaps are said thoughtlessly but are nevertheless said, do not engender hate and suspicion in the minds of those about whom we speak. We are too free in making snap judgments about other nations; that is one of the things working against international goodwill, and when our people realize that we can live together without criticizing one another, and that each nation can have its own peculiar customs without being made the butt of ridicule and criticism from other nations, then it seems to me we will have laid at least one stone of the foundation of international goodwill. So, Mr. Chairman, although I speak very earnestly, I believe sincerely that when I come to parliament-and I am going to discuss the whole subject if I may be permitted to do so, for a few minutes, since that is what other members have done-and instead of

Supply-Defence-Cadet Services
busily arming, as my good friend from Bow River suggests, I ask this House to be good enough to grant to His Majesty a sufficient sum of money to provide one permanent force soldier for every 3,000 inhabitants of the Dominion of Canada; when I ask that they grant a sufficient sum of money to provide for the training for about nine days of one citizen out of every 300 in this country, it seems to me that after all the charge of being busily arming can be harly sustained. It seems to me that I have been about as modest in my requests as I can be, and notwithstanding the opinions which have been very freely expressed around this chamber by those who, if they were asked, would not sincerely pretend to be military experts and who do not claim to have studied international conditions in order to know exactly the circumstances surrounding us which make it necessary for us to arm-notwithstanding these opinions I do prefer to take, as I should, the opinions of those who advise me in connection with this matter, and they advise me that this is the minimum which any self-respecting and self-reliant country in our position should expect to (provide for its defence services.
Now let me give the figures whish were mentioned by the hon. member for Bow River, and when he talks about busily arming let us just compare ourselves for a moment with the other countries of the world. I know that in continental countries conditions are distinctly different, because of their situation, but I think we should know exactly where we stand in relation to the other countries of the world. A comparison will show that the percentages of the total budgets of the different countries, together with the amount per head devoted to their defence forces, is as follows:

else. We have talked a lot about the professional militarists of this country, although I think perhaps only one hon. member used the expression. But, when my hon. friends speak in that way I do not think they s.re being altogether fair to the men who make up these defence forces, so-called, of this country, and I want hon. members to know what is being done in that regard. I realize these things now as I did not realize them before, because I want to tell lion, members quite frankly that I was not a member of the militia; I knew nothing of the non-permanent active militia, and was not aware of the interest which was taken in these matters by the citizens of this country generally. When I began to make inquiries I found that the men who were in command of or who were officers of units, and even those who were simply friendly to units, were giving freely of their time and money in order that the interests of these units might be secured and that the support of the men might be maintained. I found further, strange to relate, that in a great many instances the money which is being voted for the pay of these officers and men of the militia was not being drawn by them at all, but was taken by them and put into this pool, into a regimental fund, as they said in order to provide comforts and attractions for the men. I know of one particular commanding officer who spent no less than $3,000-he is only commanding the battalion for three years-in order to take his men on a little trip, and I understand, he proposes to do the same this year. So I had a questionnaire sent out to the various districts to find out how general this thing was. I have before me a table 'giving the result and, to put it briefly, it is this: We have in Canada altogether, in artil- ' lery, cavalry, infantry, signal corps, and everything, 870 units. In 219 of these units 24 per cent, both officers and men, pool all their pay and do not draw any of it at all. In 57 of the units the pay is pooled by the officers, while they draw nothing whatever themselves. In some other units part of the pay of the officers and men is pooled, running from five per cent to one hundred per cent. That applies to 79 units in all, and in 47 units, that is 5J per cent, a portion of the pay of the officers is pooled; making, in all, a total of nearly 50 per cent of the militia units of Canada in which

Supply-Defence-Cadet Services
the officers and men pool the whole or a portion of their pay. I do feel that people ought to realize that: They ought to recognize that there are men in this country just as honest and sincere in their views and just as desirous of the peace of the world as any others, who feel that they should give their time and their money in order that Canada may have, in some respects, what they consider to be an adequate defence force, and I pointed out the limitations of that force, which I do not think hon. members of this committee perhaps realize.	'
Now I have spoken of the general subject, and the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland) asked me to give some brief particulars of the matter in connection with which there are increases. I will just run over them in the hope that perhaps it may supply hon. members with information so as to avoid discussion when the items come up; but I assure hon. members that I shall be only too happy, if they think it necessary, to give all the information which can be given in connection with them when the proper -time arrives. With regard to the $100,000 increase for cadet services, I have already stated that it is required to provide for the authorization of 49 cadet units which have been organized for the past year. Sixteen of these are in the province of Quebec, which province by the way has a considerable majority of the units in Canada, and splendid units they are. The increase of $100,000 is in order to provide for the expenses of these units for the past year, and to furnish money to meet their expenses during the present year as well as to meet the normal increase in the cadet service. It is for that purpose and for nothing else.
The increase of $237,000 in connection with engineer services and works-I am mentioning only the larger items-is in order that we may do what is absolutely necessary to preserve our property in this country, and see that it does not go into absolute rack and ruin. I have had a statement prepared showing the value of the property which we hwe in Canada, and I find that there is 2i per cent, or somer thing like that, of an allowance for depreciation in connection with the juildings which the department own. I want to say that the vote which I felt I should ask for was an amount of over $1,000,000; but I realize that the House has not been making large votes in this respect, and I endeavoured to cut it down in every way possible. Therefore the amount in question has been finally agreed upon and submitted to the House for its approval. In connection with military property-I may as well mention the fact now-
I find there is a considerable amount which I think can be disposed of. I shall be only too happy to take the matter up during the coming summer, but I want hon. members of the committee to remember that although the Department of National Defence itself owns the property, the moment it is disposed of the money goes into the hands of the Receiver General. I am endeavouring personally to get in touch with the whole situation as to the property of the department, which runs straight across the country, and will then come to a sound conclusion, in the light of the best advice I can get, as to the advisability of retaining some of these properties.
With regard to general stores, the increase there is logical. It is due to the fact that the stores of clothing we had during the war are now practically exhausted, and we have to buy more. It is not because we are preparing for another war; it is only that we may have sufficient stock in order to outfit the force that we have.
The next increase is in connection with the non-permanent active militia, and the increase has to do with the training of the force. I have felt, and I think it was generally felt throughout Canada, that the most which this country can hope to do is to train a small skeleton of officers and non-commissioned officers. We cannot hope to train any more, a very large body of men, and we are not trying to do that. But we have to have enough men to make a camp, and1 to make it possible for officers and non-commissioned officers to train, and to have their training made effective. A'l'l over this country there are rural units that have not been to camp for two or three years. We cannot send them to camp-I am sorry the vote does not permit of that-but I am endeavouring to make some further provision so that, a limited number of men may possibly be taken into camp for a short time, and hope to be able to include in that some of the rural units. With that object in view I am hoping to look over the list of units. I do not want hon. members to carry this statement home to their constituents and say that this or that unit is going to be disbanded. Whatever is done in connection with this matter, although we have a most modest force, should be done along the lines of efficiency and I would rather have an infinitesimally small force, possessing efficiency and some esprit de corps, than spread1 my butter too thin all over the Dominion. The increase in this vote is to have a limited

Supply-Defence-Cadet Services
number of men in camp and make it possible for a certain number of officers and noncommissioned officers to be there.
As regards the increase to the naval service, I will give the details when that comes up. I will also deal with the vote for the air force in the same way. I will merely point out to the hon. member for Bow River that with respect to the 83,000,000 about which he is so shocked, 82,000,000 of it is taken up in the increase in the air force vote, and the greater part of it is in connection with what we call civil operations.	When the time
comej I will endeavour to go over these items with any hon. gentleman who cares to have the information. I have gone over them a/lready with the officers of the department. I have had the recommendation of the civil committee on air operations, and I think we shall be able to satisfy the House that that vote is necessary and sound, and is in the interest of this country.
Now I come back to the cadet vote. My hon. friend for Southeast Grey suggests the cadet movement began with Sir Frederick Borden. But it really dates back to 1862, and at the time Sir Frederick Borden was head of the department over which I have the honour now to preside, there were 100 cadet units in the Dominion. Very soon after that what we know as the Strathcona trust, to which the hon. member for Southeast Grey referred on Saturday, was formed. The Strathcona trust was created to carry out the provisions of a trust fund established by the late Lord Strathcona, amounting first to 8400,000 and afterwards to $500,000, and these wore the objects of the. fund as set out by the trustees:
Not only to improve the physical and intellectual capabilities of the children by inculcating habits of alertness, orderliness and prompt obedience, but also to bring up the boys to patriotism, and to a realization that the first duty of a free citizen is to be prepared to defend his country.
I could go on and read further objects, but that is sufficient for my purpose. I am glad to say that my native province of Nova Scotia was the first to combine cadet training and physical training, and that was before the Strathcona trust, was organized. Immediately Sir Frederick Borden sent out a circular under date of November 10, 1909, in wlhich he invited the cooperation of the school authorities in the various provinces.
This circular reads:
With regard, however, to the question of military drill and rifle practice for boys, a somewhat important misapprehension appears to exist in certain quarters, to the effect that the Strathcona Trust is designed to be used as

the vehicle for the introduction of compulsory military training into the schools of the Dominion. I am directed to state, emphatically, that such is in no wise Lord Strathcona's intention, nor that of the executive council of the trust.
As stated above, one of Lord Strathcona's main objects is to inculcate a spirit of patriotism in the youths of this country, together with a realization of their duty as free citizens in its defence, and, consequently, their training in the rudiments of a soldier's art is, in his opinion, desirable, in order that they may be able to give proper expression to that spirit in time of national danger; but His Lordship does not seek to insist that this military training should be made compulsory. All he asks is that the government of a province should undertake to encourage, as far as possible, the formation of cadet corps and the practice of rifle shooting in the schools under its control, leaving it to the parents themselves to decide whether their sons should join these corps. The proper military instruction and care of the cadets corps when formed is a matter which falls within the province of the Department of Militia. The Department of Militia, however, asks that the educational authorities will encourage, or, at least, place no obstacle in the way of their teachers becoming officers of their school cadet corps.
He goes on with the other conditions What was the result?	I have under my
hand agreements or memoranda signed by the educational authorities of every province in the Dominion except Quebec, and as regards Quebec I have under my hand the minutes of the Protestant committee of tlhe Council of Public Instruction and a Catholic committee of the Council of Public Instruction, both agreeing to the terms and agreeing to carry them out. Quebec has made the greatest strides of any province in the Dominion in regard to this matter of cadet training. Here is a memorandum signed by the provincial authorities of Manitoba and dated at Winnipeg, March 22, 1911:
The education department encourages the formation of cadet corps including the practice of rifle shooting under suitable conditions by the older boys, in all educational establishments under its control. A boy, however, before joining a cadet corps must first obtain his parents' or his guardian's consent.
Later the province of Manitoba sent a letter in which they said that they left it free to the individual school to make the application, but tlhey did not in any way suggest that the terms of this agreement were to be repudiated. Further than that I may say in connection with Manitoba that Mr. Fletcher, I think the deputy minister of education, is a member of tlhe committee of the Strathcona Trust which adminsters this trust from time to time.

I think it is because of the free and, I think, improper use of that word, that some of us have got very far on the wrong track. that situation, where it is optional with the parent, optional with the school, and optional with the province, and when the physical training accounts for pretty nearly three-fifths of this vote, I submit that the criticisms which have been offered have not perhaps the foundation which they might appear to have had when lion, members first addressed this House.

speechtext:
With the explanation and defence of these estimates that has been made by the Minister of National Defence I find myself in perfect accord. As one who has had actual experience of war, I want to assure the members of this House that I do not stand and speak as I shall do this afternoon in favour of cadet training because I love war. I do not at any time expect that my course will lead any boy or any citizen of this country to undertake tasks or training or sacrifice with the spirit of hate, murder or destruction in his heart. Those of us who have seen three or four years of actual warfare resent very much the words which have been used in this chamber to the effect, that these votes are passed especially for the preservation and maintenance of men with jobs. I want to say that the men at the head of that splendid Canadian corps were not experienced or practical military men. They were men who had realized in years gone by that a part of our citizenship was the necessary preparation for the maintenance and defence of that citizenship. As a member of the medical corps which in twenty-four hours had passed through its hands 5.900 wounded, it would be the last wish of mine, and I believe of the whole medical corps, that war should ever again be participated in by this or any other country. But as the minister says, we must look at these things from the practical and common sense standpoint.
We have listened to many speeches in this chamber denouncing war, but I fail to find one who has had experience in the sacrifice and has been in the service opposing the meagre amount requested by the Minister of National Defence for the protection of this country. The hon. member for Southeast Grey has been most aggressive in her opposition to these estimates, not merely this year but on many occasions. The hon. member and her supporters persist in setting up a case simply to be knocked down. I do not believe that any person connected with cadet training has * any idea of making militarists of the citizens of this country, if by the word militarist you mean one who seeks war, one who seeks by hate to murder and destroy, but that is the case conjured up against cadet training by those who are opposing this vote.
The minister, I believe, went to the root of the matter when he read the Strathcona regulations stating that the object in cadet training is a twofold one. In the first place, it is to teach the boy that he is a unit of the country. This work implies a twofold duty on the country and on the men in connection with the care of boys. One is the teaching of patriotism, the idea that he belongs to a country, and the first principle to be inculated in that boy is the lesson that it is his duty to protect his country. I know no country that' has ever become great, or that has ever been established as a nation of some reputation, which has not made this the primary teaching in the education of the boy. Above family, above individual interests, there is the interest of his native land, bis country, and as a citizen it will be his first duty to protect that country. The next duty is that he has been given a body endowed with certain functions and it is his duty to develop that body along the best lines. I think it is accepted by every person that if we could place two schools together, one having physical training, or cadet training as they like to call it, and the other without it, the result would impel every parent in the country to ask for physical or cadet training for their boys. There is no mother that I know of who does not wish to see her boy develop physically along right lines, and if there is a defect, if there is a weakness in his respiratoa-y tract or digestive tract, that that should be removed; and I know of nothing that will remove it so quickly as physical training. These two things lie at the bottom of all physical and cadet training. Greece, Rome and Sweden all adopted this system of training. At one time Sweden was the most militaristic country in the world. She has established herself now, she is still carrying on the training, and it is her system which we have adopted. In fact no country is so well known or highly respected for its physical training as Sweden, notwithstanding the remarks of the bon. member for Southeast Grey (Miss Macphail).
The opposition to this vote is based on something more serious than we see at first. I cannot help bringing this out, and I believe it is the duty of every member in this House to

Supply-Defence-Cadet Services
look beyond the mere verbal opposition to these votes. There are principles deeply rooted in the systems of those who speak against it. Shriek after shriek has gone through the chamber, demanding to know against whom are we arming. I know of nobody arming in this country. I know no work of arming against any country, because I realize .that every nation that has fallen has done so from causes within the nation and not from without. Histoiry has shown that those who decry their constitution and country and race, who teach the people wrong principles, who would sacrifice loyalty and patriotism, who would sell tradition and make easy the way of our enemy, are the people we fear most in regard to all our considerations of defence. Those are the people who are ready to open the doors for our enemies, to lull to sleep public opinion, and it is now time and I believe this is the place to speak about it. If the present Minister of National Defence had been in this House during the last four years he would have found a spirit with which he could not have agreed, and I am glad now that one with experience and one who seems to have some weight has come forward to improve conditions as they exist in this country.
I should like to dTaw attention of the members of this House not only to speeches which have been made in this chamber, but also to a matter which has been much talked of in this country within the last few days. I refer to a letter which has been written, and which profoundly affects this subject, because this is the kind of insidious secret work that tends to destroy national spirit and to interfere with those who would like to protect their country and their native land!. I propose to read this letter clause by clause.

Mr. Chairman,
when the House rose at six o'clock I had expressed my complete agreement with the words of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston); I had approved of the spirit of the Strathcona trust fund and of the twi principles which underlay the granting o! that fund, namely, the inculcation in ou: youths of the spirit of patriotism and loyalty the willingness to sacrifice themselves if necessary in the defence of their country and the willingness to develop their bodies and minds, which are claimed to be the results of cadet and physical training.
I had also dealt with the speeches delivered in this connection, and had expressed my opinion that there was something behind the verbal opposition to these grants. While we admit and grant to every person the privilege of their own opinions so far as service to the country is concerned, yet we do not grant the privilege of interfering with and taking unfair advantage of our young people. In this connection I made mention of a letter which was sent to me by a lady in the constituency of Southeast Grey, which letter I intend first to read and then to analyse. The letter is dated Ottawa, March 28, 1927. and is as follows:
Dear Teacher and Pupils:
This letter we will talk about the Chinese war. The Chinese use a great deal of a drug called opium. It is a very bad drug, much worse than liquor on the person who takes it. It gives them pleasant dreams; they live in a sort of a dream world, and are very happy, but when the influence has worn off they are nervous wrecks, and are sick. Then they want more opium to make them nice dreamers again, and if they do this thing for some time, it spoils their health, and they are not any good for anything. There was a war in China between 1839 and 1842, which is called the Opium war. The Chinese wanted to make the use of opium in China illegal, to keep it out of China, but Great Britain insisted that the Chinese government make the use of opium legal, because Great Britain own India and India sells opium to China. This made the Chinese angry. Then, too, nearly all the great ports where the big ships come in are controlled by Great Britain, or some great power like Japan, and in these Chinese cities the Chinese have no vote. The police are foreigners, the "whole show" is run by people who are not Chinese, and the Chinese have no rights.
The Chinese revere their dead, and their graveyards are a very sacred place. When western civilization came they ran railroads through the graveyards. This made the Chinese mad; and caused them to rebel. This rebellion was called the Boxer rebellion. The Chinese were defeated in this rebellion, and made to pay money called an indemnity, and Great

Supply-Dejence-Cadet Services
Britain, to make sure she got this money imposed a five per cent tax-that is, five cents on the dollar-on goods coming in. This is called customs tariff. She always controls the post offices.	.	.
Many countries, Japan, Great Britain, and before the war, Germany, had factories in the big cities of China. The living conditions in these factories are horrible; the children work as young as six years, and are often hurt and killed. The Chinese government can do nothing because these are European factories and the * owners of the factories will do nothing. A group of Chinese students walked the streets of one of their big cities about a year ago as a protest against the awful conditions of the children in factories, and the British police shot them down. You can quite easily see how all these things made the Chinese determined to put the British out of their country to bind their many provinces together in one federal government, to control their own customs, tariff and their own post offices, their own railways, etcetera. Russia, seeing that a rebellion was coming in China, wisely gave up all her rights within that country, and the Chinese are very grateful. There is little doubt that Russia is urging the Chinese to rebellion, but the conditions in China are so bad that one cannot wonder that these people rise in rebellion. Germany used to have much control in China, but according to the peace treaty of the Great war, she was forced to give up her privileges. I wish very much that Canada, who is a member of the League of Nations, would protest against what has been done in China. We have a right to try to stop anything that is breaking the peace of the world. We must remember that it is only a few very rich people in England who want to do these dreadful things in China, that most of the British people are very sad and grieved over what is being done, and that meetings are being held there in protest and some of the leading papers are saying that the action of the government and the big interests is all wrong and so we are in good company if we do say that we think the Chinese are being unfairly treated.
Many of the patriotic Canadians say over and over again, "We want Canada for Canadians". Then, if that is true, why do we not want China for Chinese? We send missionaries to teach them of Jesus, and his love, but unless we love them and act toward them as brothers, how- can they know that we believe in Jesus and his love to all.
Thursday was my birthday and I had a lovely birthday party. We have two hours for dinner between six and eight. I had a party of fourteen. I got lovely flowers, three dozen roses, three boxes of candy, some nice maple sugar, hand-kerchiefs, and all sorts of good things.
I had a very gay time. My office has been much brighter with the flowers. The gardener of the House of Commons keeps flowering plants on my window, but the roses are even more beautiful than they are.

Mr. ROSS (Kingston); Nonsense? Before I am through I will prove my assertion. It is nothing less than a distortion of historical facts, and I know nothing worse than to place such a distortion before pupils in order to give them a lesser opinion of their race, of the constitution under which they live, and of the empire with which they are connected.
Now I want' to take this letter up paragraph by paragraph. The first paragraph deals with the Chinese war, and it goes back to the time of 1839 and 1845, and to a war to which the name " opium war " is given. Now there are none except those who wish to strike at and injure Great Britain who will call that war the " opium war." There is just enough truth in it, it had just enough connection with opium, to allow some person to make the statement without being open to the charge of asserting a complete untruth, and I want to give the facts as far as I can take them from history. The issue is one of Chinese cosmogony more than anything else. It is claimed by the Chinese that' the emperor and his immediate advisers are direct sons of heaven, and when a request was made by outsiders to trade with their country, the Chinese took the attitude that trade was an inferior thing for them and they could not touch it. " Therefore," they said, " you must not go near Pekin; you must stay and trade in Canton, the farthest city away from Pekin, where you will be under the Canton officials."
The second issue in the war was this: There was a claim for port rights, and for the regulation of ports. The right to trade was granted. Before the British came there were Portuguese and there were Dutch trading there, but they had never been able to secure what they called 'treaty rights. There was also some demand for a schedule of customs. Up to this time it was up to the Canton officials to put on any customs duty they liked; to enforce a certain tax against a nation one day, another the next day or the next week to apply a different one. There was also the question of extra territoriality. That' means that the Chinese demanded the right to try a British subject, or any foreigner who was in that porit. There is a very celebrated case of where a salute was being fired and a gunner was charged with having killed a Chinaman. The Chinese demanded that this gunner be brought before them. For some time their demand was resisted, but under duress Captain Elliott, a very weak official who was in charge of British affairs in Canton at the time, handed this gunner over to the Chinese, their demand being that he should appear before them and offer an explanation. What was the result? The gunner was immediately

strangled. From that day Britain adopted a different attitude anad never permitted any British subject to be tried by Chinese authorities. She was not autocratic about this because she accepted the situation later and said: "If you will establish Chinese courts, and will satisfy us as to the fairness of those courts then we have no reason to oppose it." These were the questions that brought on this war. But opium played some part in the matter. For years opium had been brought into China from India, not by Britain only but by the Chinese themselves. For every British vessel there were thousands of Chinese vessels engaged in the trade. Many long years before, there had been a law passed against' the importation of opium but here was the situation: Opium was being brought in, not by the British but by their own people, and the son of the Canton governor was the biggest bootlegger in the business at the time.

The Queen of England desires that her subjects who may go into foreign countries should obey the laws of those countries; and Her Majesty does not wish to protect them from the just consequences of any offences which they may commit in foreign parts. But, on the other hand, Her Majesty cannot permit that her subjects residing abroad should be treated with violence, and be exposed to insult and injustice: and when wrong is done to them, Her Majesty will see that they obtain redress.
That is the reason for that war of 1839-42. Great Britain realized and took the position that her subjects must be protected wherever they were. As regards the question whether the Boxer rebellion was due to railroads being built through graveyards, I want to read from the Story of the Nations, the History of China. In this book it will be found that at this very time the Dowager Empress of China was in charge of affairs in Pekin. The item under discussion is cadet training. There is an attempt throughout this country to mislead the children of our schools and to prevent them from joining or having any sympathy with cadets corps. I have been dealing with a letter written to all the schools in a certain constituency with the intention of encouraging this opposition. In that letter it was pointed out as a reason for preventing children from joining or having sympathy with cadet corps, that there were in China factories in which children under six years of age were employed and that these factories were all run by Great Britain; that as a result of that certain students in protest marched through the streets and Great Britain shot them down. This is an absolute distortion of historical facts made apparently with the deliberate attempt to mislead the judgment of the children, to wean them away from a spirit of loyalty and patriotism, which is a spirit that should be encouraged in this country and not destroyed. I say that those students were not marching there in protest against child labour in British factories, but they were marching in protest against the killing of a Chinese by a Japanese citizen, and in marching through the streets they took occasion to make themselves obnoxious to the British section of that city. The whole letter I might say is a continued distortion of historical fact, in order to warp the children's minds and to wean them away from a sympathetic relationship with Great Britain and the empire generally.
There is also an attempt in this letter to lead the children to believe that only the influence of the rich counts in Great Britain. There is no attempt to justify the position in which Great Britain found herself in China, which was this:	Great Britain was the
champion of all the foreign elements in China, and she had to take upon her shoulders the burden of the whole situation. I think Great Britain came out of at with great credit to herself, because not only did she establish in China a customs tariff that was fair to all, but she insisted upon the post office administration and revenues being entirely under 
Chinese rule. But those facts which are creditable to Great Britain have not been touched upon in this letter. On the contrary, anything discreditable that can possibly be laid on the shoulders of Great Britain is mentioned, to wean the sympathy of the children away from Great Britain. So much for this attempt, which I believe will be resented throughout the Dominion just as much as it was resented by this lady who sent the letter to me, and who believes (that this House is the proper place to deal with this matter. In my opinion the permission of the school boards should first have been obtained before this letter was allowed to be read in the school by teachers.
I want now to take up in general some statements that have been made in this debate. It has been said that men whose jobs are in this movement are at the bottom of the demand for these estimates and for this cadet training. I want to say to this House that soldiers and trained men are the last people in the world to cause any war. Wars, we know, have been caused by politicians, not by soldiers and trained men. It has also been pointed out that England was prepared in the last war. How well prepared was England in the last war? If it had not been that all the nations joined together against the enemy, preparation would have won out. England was not prepared, and for that want of preparation 100,000 trained men laid down their lives in an attempt to stay the onrush of the enemy until some kind of training had been done.
It has also been s^ked, what has war ever done for anybody? Well, we might go back to Britain, and say that in Britain's wars she has established liberty and equality in most parts of the world. We can say also that there are some wars which have been brought about for religious and moral reasons. The Covenanters fought for moral and religious reasons, and secured results satisfactory to them. Cromwell fought for moral and religious reasons, and won out. Again, a great war was fought in the United States for the abolition of slavery, and I do not believe that that fight could have been won in any other way.
In conclusion, I want to point out as a reason for passing these estimates the new position in which we now find ourselves. We are asked to expend a small amount here in the way of the defence of our country. It has been declared by the last Imperial conference that we have an equality of status with Great Britain and every other dominion in the empire. Now if we are the equal of every

I do not hold with some criticisms that have been made of the premier of Australia and others who have come to Canada and made speeches in this country. I think it is up to us tcnday to ask the Prime Minister of this country, and I think it is up to every member of the empire to ask the Prime Minister and the government of Canada, what is our position at the present time with respect to empire defence. Have we not some little share to take in the protection of the interests of this empire and the lives of our citizens? I think we had better get back to the old principle that we are in the empire, that we belong to the races which make up the empire, and that we must take our share of responsibility for its defence. I hold that this government, in view of that declaration of equality of status, should satisfy the people oi this country and the other members of the empire as to what our position will be in regard to the defence of the empire, and if that is done I think that the majority in this House will be, like myself, in accord with the Minister of National Defence, believing that we are only doing our duty in assuming the training of some part of our citizenship in the protection of this country and of the empire. I would regret if we ever lost sight ol that first principle, and that a child should fail to realize that he belongs to a country, and that his first duty is to defend that country, because that is the basis of all these estimates; it is the principle upon which they are founded. I am sure that we will do credit not only to ourselves but to posterity and to our ancestry if we take upon ourselves this responsibility.

It is also declared to be the friendly right of each member of the league to bring to the attention of the assembly or of the council any circumstance whatever affecting international relations which threatens to disturb international peace or the good understanding between nations upon which peace depends.
And so Canada would be well within her right in protesting against anything that tends to endanger the peace of the world. There was an interesting report in the McGill Daily, a student's paper issued at McGill university, of a speech recently made, by Captain Brace-who I believe was connected with the Young Men's Christian Association and who is a returned man-on conditions in China at the present time. He said:
The cause of the trouble in China to-day is the white man, who exploits the oriental and breaks all laws of civilization in doing so.
We as Britishers must take our just share as a consequence of so serious a charge. I want to close this defence, if it can be called a defence, of my letter to the public school (Children of Southeast Grey by quoting again from Bertrand Russell. He says this, in relation to the forces going out to China:
If we were fighting for a great cause, the prospect of loss might be faced with heroism. But the exact opposite is the case: We are fighting against everything progressive, upright, and intelligent in China, in favour of everything ignorant, reactionary and corrupt. We are fighting to keep civilization under in a great nation, in order that it may be the easier to exploit. We are fighting for the right to shoot down young unarmed students when they protest against the killing of Chinese workers by Japanese capitalists in labour disputes. We are fighting to prolong anarchy and civil war among self-seeking militarists dependent upon foreign support. We are fighting to preserve everything that is bad and to prevent the growth of everything that is good. This, alas, is our position throughout Asia. This is the ' sacred cause which we pursue with a pigheaded obstinacy that must, before long, bring ruin and national disaster upon us. Both as a patriot and as an internationalist, I view tho situation with feelings little short of despair.
I want to say, regardless of what the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Ross) and the hon. member for Frontenac-Addington, (Mr. Edwards) may think, that I consider myself a patriot. I have no desire in the world to mislead the school children of Southeast Grey, or the school children of Canada, or the people of Canada on any question whatever. To the extent that any details of the letter were inaccurate I regret it, but the spirit of the letter was true and I stand by it be the consequences what they may.

The minister says that the educational institutions and the parents are free to accept or to refuse the offer of the government. But knowing how things work, one realizes that, with the object of giving physical training to their children, people are being led into accepting, against their wishes, this military organization. In some institutions, in Quebec, the organization of cadet corps was presented to the people exclusively from the point of view of physical training, and it was accepted as such. Both the parents and the children were induced to accept it; then the cadet corps were formed, and once started, once the rifles had been received from the government, they were kept up.
As I said at the beginning, I am not prepared to say that the cadet corps organization is in itself a source of militarism in its most obnoxious form. For instance, take a country like Switzerland. I do not suppose there is any other democratic country in the world so thoroughly peaceful, and where, at the same time, such attention is given to inducing all classes of the population from youth to old age to prepare themselves for the defence of their country. Once we have a standard of national patriotism well inculated in the minds of our population, then of course we will have to do something in the way of preparing our youth for the defence of their country. But in the uncertain state of mind in which we have been for the last twenty-five years, not knowing whether the duty of our people is to defend our country, or to go out and fight wars that have no relation to national defence, then everything which tends to the development of the military mind, to inducing the youth of

I do not want to say any more on the subject at the present time, because I think it is rather unfortunate that the whole scope of our military policy and foreign military ventures should have been brought under discussion on this item.
In Quebec many people are in a state of disquiet at the ultimate result of this training of the youth in our colleges. Undoubtedly it does not immediately make for the worst kind of militarism. I admit with the minister that even with some of our young men it has a better effect; it teaches them a sense of discipline which, if we are to have some kind of military organization, is certainly better than the kind of militarism which is developed at the approach of war or during war with no sense of discipline, when all sorts of inducements are held out to get untrained people to enlist. But there is also this other consequence. Once boys have been accustomed in colleges to military training, they get into their minds, precisely as is mentioned in that report of the 'Strathcona trust which the minister read, the idea that military duty is the primary duty of citizenship. It is against that spirit that a growing number of Canadian fathers of families are protesting, men who are thinking of the future of their sons and of their country, men who believe that the future of this countiy depends, not upon following the footsteps of European nations, but, on the contrary, on this generation taking full advantage of the dour experience of the war to induce our people to work for peace, to realize that their best contribution to the peace of the world is to make peace at home not only possible, but if we can, to make it unavoidable, to make the world understand through the League of Nations of which we form a part, that Canada is not prepared to follow any country, foreign or British, in launching the world once again into military ventures such as those through which the world has passed Therefore I think it is time, not only to talk of peace, but to work for peace. It is not sufficient to say that this military training has been going on for twenty or thirty years, and that the minister is simply asking for a small increase to meet new requests. If this government meant what it said through its representatives at Geneva and London, namely that it is prepared to help the British government, the governments of the other dominions and foreign nations in the development of a spirit of peace, it should

begin at home and show in the estimates and in dealing with the public money that Canada means peace in fact and not only in words.
Therefore, instead of encouraging the development of those cadet corps in the colleges, we should on the contrary work towards changing that organization into a purely peaceful one of physical training. If it comes to that, then we have to remember the order of things as it was created and as it is maintained by our constitution. Everything which relates to civil education belongs to the provinces. This government and this parliament should have no business to come into the various educational institutions in this country and take the lead in introducing one branch of training into any educational institution. We have heard very often from the other side eloquent and even ferocious pleas in regard to absolute provincial autonomy in matters of education. Why should the federal government step in and subsidize physical training, if we mean only to prepare the youth of the country for the works of peace? But if this is connected with military organizations, if we are taking advantage of the trust first, and these estimates afterwards, to encourage the development of a military spirit in the colleges, then the minister must admit that the objection raised by the hon. member for Southeast Grey is well founded; that this government is stepping out of its normal functions; that it is entering into a field which is under the control of the provinces in order, through those institutions and under the pretence of physical training, to instil into our youth the spirit of militarism. I do not say that it is the worst kind of militarism; I do not say that all these young men will go out from these colleges with the idea of killing and murdering; I do not go to that exaggeration; but undoubtedly it creates in their minds what prepares them in after life to respond to the call of militarism. It turns their mind in that direction. Therefore I support the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Southeast Grey, first because I think it is logical that we should invite the provinces out of their own funds to look after the matter of physical training, and secondly because I do not believe it is the duty of this government to take advantage of the sj'stem of physical training to introduce military training into the educational institutions.
With regard to the option of parents, I might give this information to the minister. I know of at least one, and I presume it is only one out of many, educational institution in the province of Quebec where they started with the idea of having physical training, but

I should like to

This afternoon the hon. member for Frontenac-Addington made an attack upon me; he went into the history of the Winnipeg strike. From my standpoint his statements entirely misrepresent the situation. I had no chance to protest against them. Further than that, he entirely misrepresented my connection with that strike. I do not think it is necessary for me to go into the matter tonight, but I might say that on one date which he quoted, on the 17th of May of that year, I was on the Pacific coast when these things were happening in Winnipeg, and' I had absolutely nothing to do with what oc-cured in Winnipeg at that date.' I do not want to go into that matter to-night, but I could, I think, put up a very strong case for the workers. May I merely suggest in passing that one hon. member of the House last year who attacked me on that matter is not in the House this year, and the vote to-day showed that I had the support of the entire Winnipeg and Manitoba group who happened to know the situation much better than do the people in the east. I do not want to be too hard on outsiders with regard to this matter, because I know that propaganda
was sent out through the press that misrepresented the entire situation. However, I leave that to one side.
I was anxious to speak on this question to-night because the vote on the Chairman's ruling this afternoon was not taken on the point to which I had raised objection, and I had no opportunity then of setting myself right. Later on, after the vote was taken, the hon. member for Frontenac-Addington-I want to give him credit-gave a fairly accurate statement of the case, but I think there was a decided misunderstanding on his part as well as on the part of the chairman as to just where my objection lay, so I want to make that clear. The hon. member for Frontenac-Addington quoted from what he said was a speech of mine. I think it was in reality a quotation from the preamble of the platform of the Labour party of British Columbia of which I was then a member, and where I happened then to be living. It runs as follows:
The ultimate object of the confederated labour party is the collective ownership and democratic operation of the means of wealth and production. This involves a complete revolution in our whole economic and social structure.
Apparently the word "revolution" frightened or scandalized the hon. member for Frontenac-Addington. I might point, out to him that according to the historians there took place in Great Britain about one hundred and fifty years ago what was known as the industrial revolution; that was the change from hand production to machine production. Every student of historj' knows that revolution is a term constantly used in industrial history and economics. A great many of us in the labour movement who have tried to study historical developments are of opinion that sooner or later the industrial revolution must be . followed by an economic revolution, meaning a change in our way of controlling this huge machinery of production. I think I would be speaking in terms that would be best comprehended by gentlemen here if I should say that we believe that in the days to come public ownership is inevitable, and if you change from private ownership of a lot of little concerns to public ownership on a large scale by municipalities or by the state you are bringing about what might be termed an economic revolution. That is the point of view of the Labour party, and so far from wishing to repudiate anything of that kind,
I might say that is the reason why I am in this House, for that is the platform of the Labour party both in Canada and in Great Britain. Let me read a paragraph of something

And I quoted from the platform of the British Labour party:
The view of the Labour party is that what has to be reconstructed after the war is not this or that government department, or this or that piece of social machinery, but, so far as Britain is concerned, society itself.
That is what we belive: there has to be a general social reconstruction. I commented:
"Revolutionary!" certainly. But the exponents of this view are not persecuted as British and Scotch anarchists. A goodly number of them have been elected to parliament.
Then I went on to quote further from the British Labour party manifesto:
The individualist system of capitalist production based on the private ownership and competitive administration of land and capital with its reckless "profiteering" and wage slavery; with its glorification of the unhampered struggle for the means of life, and its hypocritical pretense of the "survival of the fittest"; with the monstrous inequality of circumstances which it produces and the degradation and brutalization, both moral and spiritual, resulting therefrom may, we hope, indeed have received a death-blow.
I went on:
We must insure that what is presently to be built up is a new social order, based not on fighting, but on fraternity-not on the competitive struggle for the means of bare life, but on a deliberately planned cooperation in production and distribution for the benefit of all who participate by hand or by brain-not on the utmost possible inequality of riches, but on a systematic approach toward a healthy equality of material circumstances for every person born into the world-not on an enforced dominion over subject nations, subject races, subject colonies, subject classes or a subject sex, but, in industry, as well as in government, on that equal freedom, that general consciousness of consent, and that widest possible participation in power both economic and political, which is characteristic of democracy.
Some of us were urging upon the labour people that they ought to bring this about in this country as far as was possible by partici-

pation in politics. I do not know whether it is possible for economic changes to come about in that way, but we were urging that the labour people should take advantage of this means of advancing their cause and go into parliament. Reference was made by the hon. member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) to some statement by Mr. Ivens in which he suggested that labour should get control of the parliament buildings. He said, "We shall soon mov* in". That was a horrible thing to say! As a matter of fact, Mr. Ivens did move in before very long; he is a member of the provincial house to-day, with four or five of the men associated with him. They were urging political action. It is true that some labour men believe that the only way to bring about these social changes is by force. Some of us have taken the opposite stand. I do not know whether we are correct or not, but we have tried to oppose military force, both as a means of settling international difficulties and also as a means of settling class difficulties, and we have said frankly that we hoped that reason would prevail rather than events would be allowed to drift from bad to worse until there was a cataclysm. That has been the position we have taken. It then seems strange that the hon. member for Frontenac, when I was trying to reduce our own national armament-and I was elected on that platform, it is not only my personal view, but our party platform-should accuse me of wanting to build uip a force for political revolutionary purposes. He made a statement to which I took exception. After quoting me correctly he said words to this effect:
So the object was collective ownership and a complete revolution if necessary by such means as were undertaken in the Winnipeg strike.
That was the sentence to which I objected. I said nothing Whatever in this connection about the Winnipeg strike. I had not the Winnipeg strike remotely in my mind when at that time I used the platform of the Labour party of British Columbia. I 'had not a political revolution in my mind. I was getting *back to the question of an economic revolution which we believe should succeed an industrial revolution. The only thing that makes me wonder whether there will be a political revolution is the stupidity of many of our people who refuse to see the changes that have come about. I want to make myself clear on this. I stand for this platform which has been read several times in the House. I urge the bringing about of this platform if possible by political means; whether or not it will come about in this way largely depends,

It would therefore seem to me that we are not responding to the wishes of the conference upon which all t'he representatives agreed, by increasing the amount devoted to our militia by about 20 per cent.

speechtext:

speechtext:

maintopic: SUPPLY-OIL AND GAS RIGHTS IN WESTERN CANADA
speechtext: I do not know that I can add very much more to what I have already said. I only want to add that I think this vote is less this year than it was before the war. Perhaps some hon. members of the committee may not understand that this is purely a non-permanent active militia vote, and is only to provide for the training for nine days of about one-quarter of the paper strength of that force.

maintopic: SUPPLY-OIL AND GAS RIGHTS IN WESTERN CANADA
speechtext: I would like to ask the minister if there is any increase in establishment.

maintopic: SUPPLY-OIL AND GAS RIGHTS IN WESTERN CANADA
speechtext: No.

maintopic: SUPPLY-OIL AND GAS RIGHTS IN WESTERN CANADA
speechtext:
There is no increase in the establishment; the only thing is that you are trying to train a greater proportion of the paper strength. As one who has had some occasion to learn of the work of the militia, I desire to say that the militiamen generally, and those who are interested in the defence force of this country, approve very highly of the action of the government in this regard. The rural battalions, particularly, have not had a fair chance in regard to instruction; a very small proportion of the paper strength of the rural battalions has been instructed at all. Now if we are going to have a force, even on paper, which can be called upon for the defence of our shores, for instance-and I think the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) would not object to that-that force must be trained in order to be effective if such an occasion should unhappily arise. Instructors are sent out; militia officers have devoted their time and money almost without stint trying to make the non-permanent force
Supply-National Defence

of this country as efficient as possible. Some pay is given to officers and other ranks, but I think in almost every case that pay is turned in for the good of the service. I cannot recall a case where any rank of the militia has taken the pay allotted to him for training and devoted it to his own use; that money is diverted to the service of this country in keeping up the different militia units. In the cities, while we have a good deal of trouble, we do not face anything like the difficulties which confront rural battalions, which under the previous appropriation could only train a very few of their men. There is no building up of a military spirit, as the hon. member for Labelle knows; it is purely a matter of preparing men should the time come when our shores must be defended.
I have only a further word to say, and I say it because I am not in the militia now and therefore am not talking of anything in which I am concerned. These men who have interested themselves in the permanent force of our country are deserving of the greatest possible praise and credit for the work they have done, for their sacrifices of time and money in order to keep up in some degree the potential forces of this country. I think the hon. member for Labelle may rid his mind of the notion that this is an increase in armament, because it is not an increase in any way; it is only an attempt to make a greater proportion of that paper strength trained and effective for the purpose for which they were raised. As forcefully as I can, I desire to support this vote, knowing that it meets with the approval of those who have the interests of their country at heart, as reflected in the establishment of the non-permanent active militia.
