maintopic: SUPPLY-OIL AND GAS RIGHTS IN WESTERN CANADA
speechtext:
Perhaps I might introduce,
under this item, a resolution which has been sent to me, without going much farther afield than previous speakers have done. The resolution in question is from the Cowichan branch of the Canadian Legion of the British Empire Service League, and reads as follows:
Owing to the fact that Canada has large trade interests in China, which are likely to expand, also to the fact that there are many Canadians in China who are being protected by the imperial troops-
Be it resolved that the Canadian government be requested to pay entire costs of transport, maintenance and treatment of all imperial service men invalided to Canada from any cause whatsoever due to service in China.
I am in complete accord with this resolution. We look to the great British navy for defence in all parts of the world, but we contribute very little towards its upkeep and wre of British Columbia feel ashamed that we do not contribute more. We can call ourselves an autonomous nation or anything else we like, but the fact is that we are simply a unit of the great British nation and I am glad that such is the case. Therefore I do not see why we should not contribute some modicum towards the upkeep of that splendid navy which protects us and our ships which sail at least some of the seven seas.
When that wonderful warship the Blake sailed into Esquimalt harbour, I am sure the rank and file and officers of that ship must have been greatly impressed. Our regular army consisting of two hundred and fifty or three hundred men were there to await the arrival of those officers and men and there were perhaps one hundred and fifty others, boy scouts and naval reserve men, making a total of some five hundred men to meet that great warship. When the officers were landing, the band at the head of those men played "0 Canada, we stand on guard for thee." I am sure those men must have been favourably impressed with our Canadian regular army of three or four hundred men who stood on guard.
Those are good men, willing to do their share, all that they can do, but we think they should receive better treatment than they are receiving. We have naval reserve men, naval instructors, a number of them, men that we have borrowed from the Imperial (army. They did good work in the Imperial army; they came to Canada and gave us their services, and have a grievance in this respect; they wish the time they spent in the Imperial army added for pension purposes to the time they have given their services to Canada.

That is a reasonable attitude on their part. I took the matter up last year, but as hon. members know, in the hectic days of last session little was accomplished. I wish the department would take this matter under consideration.
I wish the department would take under consideration also the resolution which has been received from the great Canadian league. Surely we should have some national pride. We do not want protection for nothing. This "peace at any price" movement stops at the Rocky mountains; we have very little of it in British Columbia. We hold in absolute contempt men who have no national pride and who belong to the "peace at any price" party as we call them in this country. We do not want them in British Columbia, and I would suggest that we set aside at Port Nelson-and I know of no more unfavourable place-a colony to which to transport those people along with the Doukhobors and bible students. I do not know that Port Nelson will be useful for any other purpose, but it would be of some use in that regard, so let us send them there. I was going to say: Let us send a few free traders with them but when I come back to consider the matter, practically every fanatic in Canada is a free trader and therefore that branch of politics would be well represented at Port Nelson. We want no "peace at any price" people in British Columbia and we have very few of them there.
If we are part and parcel of that great British nation, let us do something towards the upkeep of the navy which protects our ships. Australia, New Zealand, and South Africa all contribute many times more than we do towards the upkeep of the British navy. Surely we have some national pride. We call ourselves a nation; we say that we have perfect autonomy. I say this is hardly correct. Some day we may have; some day we may make this a great nation and we may have complete autonomy. I know of no reason why we should wish to separate from the great British nation. We receive from them more than we do from any other people in the world; they are our best friends, and we have an immense balance of trade with them. But we take their money and hand it over to our neighbours in the United States. Some of my weak-kneed friends to the left pay that we can place reliance on the Monroe doctrine. What kind of a Canadian is one who would expect the United States to defend Canada on the seas or anywhere else? There is no need of war between Canada and the United States; the United States is at present effecting an economic conquest of this country.

Supply-National Defence
Wherever you go you see great institutions owned by United States capitalists who come to Canada because they know this is a goodly land, and they are bringing capital into this country ad lib. In British Columbia most of our pulp mills, many of our great sawmills and our mines, are under the control of United States capitalists. It is said and it has never been disputed that 70 per. cent of our timber belongs to United States people. They are effecting an economic conquest of Canada without going to war with us, as I am sure they never expect to do. I would be ashamed of any Canadian who said that we should come under the protection of the Monroe doctrine. Let us stay with the great British Empire until the time comes when we may break away and I hope that time will never come.

maintopic: SUPPLY-OIL AND GAS RIGHTS IN WESTERN CANADA
speechtext: I would like to say a word at this point, not because I am going to oppose the item, but because of the insult that has been thrown out to this part of the House by the hon. member (Mr. Dickie). Patriotism throughout British Columbia does not end at the Rocky mountains. Members in this part of the House to-day have perhaps somewhat more patriotism than the hon. member himself has. Saskatchewan was one of the first to heed the call; it sent more men to meet the enemy at the front than did British Columbia, and moreover we did not talk about it. When the hon. member throws out an insult of that kind, it is only one of many that we have had to stand this year and last year. Saskatchewan has done its share, and when the hon. member throws out a blanket insult of that kind, it hurts everybody at this end of the House. I do not have to accept a lecture from the hon. member regarding my loyalty to the British Empire. I was brought up in Great Britain and I am glad that I was. I am British to the core to-day, and 1 want to tell the hon. member that two of mine went out of my home and1 faced the enemy for three years and a half in Europe. I do not know whether the hon. member can say that or not. Whether he can or can not he is not entitled to lecture us on our patriotism.

maintopic: SUPPLY-OIL AND GAS RIGHTS IN WESTERN CANADA
speechtext: I said nothing at all against the patriotism of the hon. member.

maintopic: SUPPLY-OIL AND GAS RIGHTS IN WESTERN CANADA
speechtext:
I want these hon. gentlemen
to sit down and keep quiet while I am
speaking. As regards charging anyone in this part of the House being weak-kneed, let mo say that Saskatchewan to-day is making her own living, finding her own income and furnishing as large a part of the national income as any other province in Canada. More than that we are doing that by selling our products against the competition of the whole world, whereas the hon. member says that he cannot make a living in that way. We can do it, and to-day when we advocate peace, we are advocating peace through trade methods that will make for peace instead of war. I want the hon. gentleman to understand that when the call for war came, Saskatchewan was the first to answer, and more men while they were particularly needed, went from Saskatchewan than from any other province in Canada.

However that may be, when the question of the co-ordination of all the air forces of Great Britain and the dominions in time of war was discussed, we find that the Prime Minister made this declaration:
The organization and training of this force-[DOT]
The Canadian Air Force-
-has followed closely that of the Royal Air Force, and very substantial progress has been made. Two training centres and six stations (three temporary, during the summer months) have been established in various parts of the country, so as to carry out the several duties of the Royal Canadian Air Force.
Then later on:
Officers of the Royal Canadian Air Force are in attendance at the Air Force Staff College, Andrew, and at the Naval Staff College, Greenwich. Others are taking courses at various schools in England.
An exchange of officers has recently been arranged, and liaison visits are also carried out periodically.
Still further on the Prime Minister says:
The Royal Canadian Air Force has made commendable advances in the civil side of its work. As I mentioned at a previous session of the conference, immense areas are being surveyed annually, and millions of acres of valuable forest land protected. The work on the civil side is of such a nature that it provides practical training for the air force personnel.
Civil aviation has a direct relation to the creation of a military air force, and serves to create a reserve thereto.
By the Air Force Regulations an individual who obtains a pilot's certificate automatically becomes a reservist.
So it must be well understood that the personnel of the so-called civil air force is under the authority of the Department of National Defence, and if the Prime Minister has been correctly reported, these pilots automatically become members of the reserve. In other words, the civil air force is nothing but a training body for the preparation of a military air force, which I can understand quite well from a military point of view. Of course, if the object of this whole organization is to recruit aviators, train them for civil work and then keep them in the reserve so that in time of war they come under the authority of the Militia Act as a part of the air force, well and good. But I think the people of this country should be informed of that fact, otherwise we are simply beginning a repetition of what took place some fifteen years ago with regard to the naval force. It was represented in some parts of the country that this force was to be organized for the defence of the country, while in other quarters it was declared to be the most effective contribution Canada could make to the Imperial navy. One side was shown in Quebec, the other side was presented to Ontario, and there went on quite a good deal of equivocation which did not do much good, I think, for the moral unity of the people of this country. I hope we are not on the eve of a repetition of the same comedy of errors. If we mean to participate in the movement which some countries of Europe are undertaking, that is replacing the naval force, and to a large extent the land force, by aerial preparations, not only for the defence of the country but for participation in all imperial wars in cooperation with the British nation and the other nations of the empire, it is just as well that we should know it now. It is not a policy of peace, but at least it is a policy. If it is the policy of the government, those of us who are not in favour of such a policy should not be given to understand that this vote is merely the preparation of a civil air force and has no connec-
Supply-National Defence

tion with the military air force. If the declarations made in London are to govern our air forces-or should I say our aerial policy?-then it means that the civil organization is nothing but a preparation for a military organization. That is what is taking place in France, that is what is taking place in Italy, that is what is taking place-I think to a certain extent although I am not quite sure-in England. As to Germany, everybody in Europe knows of course that if Germany is ever in a position to take her revenge, it will be precisely by the transformation into a military force of the enormpus civil air force she is now organizing.

Nobody has ever suggested that, and there is nothing, I think, in our laws which could make it possible. But here we have an undefined position. We have a declaration here to-day that the government is contemplating a complete separation of the civil organization and the military organization; and we have a report from the Imperial conference making the Prime Minister declare in London that there is a direct and close connection between the two services, and that as a matter of fact the civil force is a reserve for the military force. speechtext: If I may be permitted, it is perfectly well known to myself, as it is to every other hon. member who is following the course of events, that there is a great deal of smuggling going on such as my hon. friend refers to, and more particularly in the maritime provinces, and I am now trying to obtain the money so that I can get the men to enable us to put a stop to that traffic. Up to the present time we have not had sufficient money to get the organization to do the work as we want to do it, and that is exactly the purpose of bringing in these estimates. Our plans are not complete, being still subject to some qualification and variation, but we propose to put along the whole boundary line of Canada and the United States, in the maritime provinces and on the seaboard, a force of men which we think will be sufficient to cope with that evil, in a reasonable way, at least. It means not only putting on a force of several hundred men, but the obtaining of vessels to be used in the prevention of smuggling. It means also the obtaining of automobiles, perhaps 25 or 30 in number, for the purpose of patrolling the border and the roads in the maritime provinces. That is the organization we propose to build up as we are able to do so once the money is voted and the men can be obtained. For the benefit of the committee I may say that the framework of the organization is fairly well completed, but we have not yet clothed it with the men and officers. I would like to have an
explanation from the minister with regard to the wholesale manner in which he is beheading postmasters in the province of New Brunswick and particularly in the so-called French counties. As I understand it, there have been cases of the most gross injustice perpetrated since the present Postmaster General took office, particularly in his own county. I have only one case in my own county; that is the case of the postmaster at Canterbury Station, but I anticipate that before the minister is in office many years I will have a great many others. The case of which I have particular knowledge is the case of a returned soldier who was appointed by the Civil Service Commission about two or three years ago, a man well qualified for the work, who served his country overseas and who was appointed because he possessed the necessary qualifications. In the same village where he lived was another person who aspired to the position at that time, but who did not succeed in getting it; he is a man who has since gone into bankruptcy and who is to-day an undischarged bankrupt. This man who was appointed has been relieved of his duty after a hearing which was nothing more than a farce; the evidence against him was that he was taking returns on election night over the telephone, and giving them out to the neighbours; that was the only offence

of a political character reported to me. I know of my own knowledge that he took no part in the election; I especially warned him not to do so, because I knew his head would come off if anything happened.

He has been dismissed with no evidence of political partisanship, in the hope of putting another man into office who has been named to the minister by the Liberal Committee of Canterbury Station, and who has been installed as temporary postmaster. He is a man who owes everybody he can owe in that community, and a man who should not and, I think, will not be appointed to the position of postmaster. I do not think he will receive the appointment because as I understand it there is another good Liberal in the community, a returned man, who is applying for the position, and I believe that in justice to that returned soldier the Civil Service Commission will appoint him rather than the other person.
A return was brought down the other day which was very interesting. I did not know these estimates were coming up to-night or I would have brought it with me to put on Hansard. It showed that from September 24 to March 28 there have been some sixty-three dismissals of country postmasters in the province of New Brunswick. That is a very large number, and they are probably all in the northern communities. I cail to mind the case of one George Chalmers, the postmaster at Charlo Station, commonly known as Charlo. I would like to explain to the House that George Chalmers is a first-class citizen and was a brother-in-law of James Reid, who for many years was a respected member of this House, sitting on the Liberal benches. If George Chalmers has any political sentiments at all they are undoubtedly Liberal, because he owed his appointment to Mr. Reid. Chalmers was dismissed, so far as I am aware, with no adequate investigation; speaking from memory, I think an inspector was sent up from Saint John, and was directed to a certain person who would give evidence against Mr. Chalmers. On the file there is a letter from that very person saying that he knows absolutely nothing as to any part taken by Mr. Chalmers in an election contest. There is also the frank admission on the part of Mr. Chalmers that he drove 
his family and some neighbours to the polls on election day, and did nothing more. I want to tell the Prime Minister that that man is not receiving justice. More than 90 per cent of the people who use that post office wish him to be retained. The general manager of a lumber company, the only mercantile firm in the community, a former member of the local legislature, has written to the department, and his letter is on file, to the effect that his company provides fifty per cent of the entire postal revenue of the office, and they abject to the dismissal of Mr. Chalmers. I think this is a case of grave injustice, and I ask the Prime Minister himself to take ten minues and look over the file, from which he will find that this man should not have been dismissed. I do not remember who has succeeded him; I do not think anyone has been appointed permanently, but the man who wanted the job has been made temporary postmaster. Ninety per cent of the people of that community have signed a petition asking that Chalmers be reinstated, and if the Prime Minister is faithful to the memory of an old supporter and old friend he will look into the matter and will not allow such an injustice to be perpetrated on Mr. Chalmers.

I do not know that it is necessary to add to what I have said in connection with these dismissals, but I will say that no administration to date, either Liberal or Conservative, has shown as much partisanship as has the present administration in dismissals of not only post office employees but also marine officials. In the parish of Salisbury, county of Westmorland, which I have the honour to represent, a number of fisheries guardians were recommended by the Liberal administration in 1926. When Mr. Meighen was called upon to form a government, I was asked to make recommendations to the department to fill these positions. My recommendations were in accord with those of the Liberal party, because it was too small a matter to bother with. When the election was over and the Liberal government returned to power, they singled out a returned soldier who had served four years in France, who had four children and who was endeavouring to make his way in the world in this manner. maintopic: SUPPLY-OIL AND GAS RIGHTS IN WESTERN CANADA
speechtext:
From 1922 onward the
policy of the late Postmaster General was not to extend the system of rural mail delivery. I have always taken the view that

Supply-Post Office
the federal government could perform no more useful service to the people in the rural communities than the extension of these routes. I know of nothing that will bring more contentment to the people in the country than having their mail delivered frequently to their doors. In my constituency- which is a fairly large one as the minister knows-there are still communities without rural mail service, and there are other communities not served often enough. I have been only able to accomplish something along this line about election time, when a little pressure produces some consideration, but afterwards no matter what party is in power they freeze up. I suppose it is because of the expense and the desire not to have a deficit. But I would impress on the minister the desirability if giving a good rural service. The cities are well served. In my [DOT] own city of ten thousand people we have three deliveries a day, but people within ten or fifteen miles are given only two deliveries a week. To-day with daily newspapers the people are entitled to a daily delivery, and I would enlist the sympathy of the Postmaster General for those people. We have a struggle to keep people on the land, and to make rural life more attractive I think nothing is more effective than rural mail delivery, telephones and good roads.

maintopic: SUPPLY-OIL AND GAS RIGHTS IN WESTERN CANADA
speechtext: For the information of the House I may say that there are 213,000 rural boxes throughout the different sections of the country, which were purchased at a cost of $800,000.

maintopic: SUPPLY-OIL AND GAS RIGHTS IN WESTERN CANADA
speechtext: But that is all reimbursed to the department.

maintopic: SUPPLY-OIL AND GAS RIGHTS IN WESTERN CANADA
speechtext: Yes. In the general estimates will be found an item of $75,000, and in the supplementaries another item of $35,000, for the purchase of rural mail boxes. We believe in extending the rural mail system as much as possible. For the information of my hon. friend from York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) I may say that only recently I issued an order for a rural delivery from Peniac in his county, although it is for the accommodation of only six or seven families.

maintopic: SUPPLY-OIL AND GAS RIGHTS IN WESTERN CANADA
speechtext: I am much obliged to the minister. I have been trying to get that for seven years.

maintopic: SUPPLY-OIL AND GAS RIGHTS IN WESTERN CANADA
speechtext: We have a number of applications from the western, central and maritime provinces. I would draw the attention of hon. members on both sides of the House to the fact that in many cases where we are asked to establish rural mail routes it is impossible because of the very low revenues. I have in mind three offices where the revenue is only $120, and to lay out a rural route cost practically $600 or $700. It is unreasonable under the circumstances to ask the department to assume that expenditure. True, the department is supposed to give the best accommodation possible and not to make any profit, but we cannot incur unreasonable deficits.

maintopic: SUPPLY-OIL AND GAS RIGHTS IN WESTERN CANADA
speechtext: The minister has referred to a feature that is not without difficulty, but I would point out that the mail service ought to be run more or less on the principle of the common school system-the rich districts should take care of the poor. The city of Moncton pays into the postal revenues over $300,000, and the city of Fredericton pays in twice as much as it costs to run the office. The thickly settled districts ought to pay for those sparsely settled. On no other principle can you establish many rural free deliveries. I am going to press for this, no matter who is Postmaster General or what party is in power, until there is a rural delivery box at the door of every farmer in my county.

maintopic: SUPPLY-OIL AND GAS RIGHTS IN WESTERN CANADA
speechtext: I would like to add just a word to what the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) has said. I have stated in this House before and I state again that if there is one department of the government which is entitled to Show a deficit without criticism it is the Post Office department. Let us look at this thing reasonably. The people of the country all contribute to building up Canada, but naturally wealth centres in the cities. These centres of population get their public works and enjoy the benefits of the money which is spent in their construction, while the only service which can be given the country districts is the rural mail service. I repeat that if there is any justification for a deficit in any department of the government in connection with services given to the public it is in connection with the service given the rural districts by the Post Office Department. I think a great deal of latitude should be allowed in serving these rural communities, because a mail service is the only thing the government can give these people to show that they are a part of the country. I appreciate the position of the Postmaster General if you want to argue this question from the standpoint of whether or not these routes will pay; in that case a good many of them will be wiped out.

maintopic: SUPPLY-OIL AND GAS RIGHTS IN WESTERN CANADA
speechtext: We cannot do that.

maintopic: SUPPLY-OIL AND GAS RIGHTS IN WESTERN CANADA

That is an unreasonable attitude.

maintopic: SUPPLY-OIL AND GAS RIGHTS IN WESTERN CANADA
speechtext: My constituency is strictly rural, and I appeal not only on behalf of that constituency, but for all rural communities. I believe they are well entitled to that consideration.

maintopic: SUPPLY-OIL AND GAS RIGHTS IN WESTERN CANADA
speechtext: I agree with you.

maintopic: SUPPLY-OIL AND GAS RIGHTS IN WESTERN CANADA
speechtext: I do not very often find myself in such hearty agreement with my hon. friends opposite, but I want to thank the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) and the hon. member for Frontenac-Addington (Mr. Edwards) for making this plea, and I do so on behalf of all the Liberal members from Saskatchewan. Last year when we came here we investigated the amount of money spent on rural mail delivery in the various provinces, and we found that the amount spent in the province of Saskatchewan was almost negligible, while New Brunswick and Ontario were reasonably well served. I quite believe that those two hon. gentlemen who have just spoken would not wish to see the rural mail delivery extended in their own provinces until Saskatchewan was brought up to their standard. That being the case we thank them for making these remarks on belhalf of rural mail delivery in Saskatchewan. Now I would like to say to the minister that in my province we believe the time has arrived when the rural mail service should be extended throughout the entire province, and when we have the same service provided in the eastern provinces we will consider ourselves reasonably well served.

maintopic: SUPPLY-OIL AND GAS RIGHTS IN WESTERN CANADA
speechtext: I just wish to say a word on behalf of the members from Alberta who are also anxious to see the rural mail routes extended. I would like to tell the minister that in my constituency we have a mail route which we would like extended; it is a very important route, and I believe he has the matter under advisement now. Then I would ask the Prime Minister if he is aware that it is now to-morrow, in fact it has long been to-morrow, and I believe it would be as well if we went home now for a little rest.

speechtext: I was going to suggest that we pass items 358 and 20 and allow item 542 of the supplementary estimates to stand over, with the understanding that we may discuss anything in this connection on that item when U is called.

speechtext:
I only wish to keep
the House a moment; we have taken up a good deal of time discussing politics in regard 
to this item, so I do not think it will hurt the House to wait and hear what I have to say. Hon. members have made a plea for the extension of the free rural delivery service, with which I am heartily in accord. We in western Canada know that we have not very much service along these lines as compared with the older sections of Canada. Of course we do not expect to get that service immediately, but we would like to see the Postmaster General give some attention to that branch of his department. There is another point, however, which I think is probably even more important, having to do with the provision of small post offices throughout the length and breadth of western Canada, where it is impossible to expect free delivery, and where the people are so isolated that they have to go thirty or forty miles for their mail. I want to make a plea for those * people. I received intimations from the Post Office Department . recently that many of these isolated post offices will be closed because of the small amount of business being done, and I do not think that is a fair proposition at all; those are the places to which I think the Postmaster General should give a good deal of consideration, even if the service does not pay.

maintopic: SUPPLY-OIL AND GAS RIGHTS IN WESTERN CANADA

I happened to receive

Those are the people for whom I wish to plead; those living close to post offices are in a position to get their mail once or twice a week, but these people who have to travel thirty or forty miles should get more consideration, even if it costs the country some money. I hope the Postmaster General will take that matter into consideration and give it his earnest attention.
